entry.title: Building an Invoice Approval Workflow with SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
A step-by-step guide to collecting invoice data through a form and routing it through a conditional, human-in-the-loop approval flow. 

Introduction 

One of the most common enterprise scenarios is: a document comes in, someone needs to review it, and a decision needs to be made. SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) is purpose-built for exactly this — orchestrating human approvals on top of business data, with no custom UI development required. 

In this post, we'll build a complete Invoice Approval workflow in BPA. An invoice form is submitted, a condition checks the total amount, and if it crosses a threshold, the invoice is routed to an approver's My Inbox as a read-only approval form with Approve/Reject actions. Once decided, an email notification is sent automatically. 

Here's what we'll cover: 

  • Designing a trigger form for invoice submission 
  • Building the process flow with a conditional branch 
  • Creating a read-only approval form for the reviewer 
  • Mapping data from the trigger form into the approval task 
  • Sending automated email notifications 
  • Configuring a mail destination for outbound email 
  • Testing the complete flow end to end 

Step 1: Create the Trigger Form (InvoiceFormSubmit) 

Every BPA process needs a way to start. Here, we use a Form Trigger — a form that, when submitted, kicks off a new process instance carrying whatever data was entered. 

  1. In your BPA project, add a new Form trigger and name it InvoiceFormSubmit. 
  1. Build out the fields to match your invoice structure: Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Supplier, Bill To, Currency, and Purchase Order. 
  1. Add a Products Details table (a repeating list) with Description, Quantity, Unit Price, and Amount columns, so multiple line items can be captured. 
  1. Add Subtotal, Tax Amount, and Total Amount fields, followed by a Contact Details section (Name and Email) so we know who submitted the invoice and who should be notified later. 

 

 

The InvoiceFormSubmit trigger form being built in the Forms editor — Invoice Details section. 

 

 

The remainder of the form — Products Details, totals, and Contact Details, with the Submit button that triggers the process. 

With the form saved, this becomes the entry point for the entire process — every field here becomes a process variable we can use downstream. 

Step 2: Build the Process Flow 

With the trigger in place, switch to the process editor and lay out the flow logic. 

  1. Drag in a Condition step right after the trigger. 
  1. Add a branch condition: Total Amount is greater than 4000. This becomes the "If" path; everything else falls to "Default." 
  1. On the If path, add a User Task (the approval form) with two outcomes — Approve and Reject. 
  1. On the Default path (amount 4000 or below), add a Send Mail step for auto-approval, so low-value invoices skip manual review entirely. 
  1. After the approval task, branch again on the outcome: Approve goes to a Send Mail (approval) step, Reject goes to a Send Rejection Mail step. Both paths converge to the End event. 

 

 

The full deployed process: InvoiceFormSubmit trigger → Condition → ApprovalForm (with Approve/Reject branches) → email notifications → End. 

 

 

Configuring the branch condition — routing only invoices with Total Amount greater than 4000 to manual approval. 

Step 3: Configure the Approval Form 

The approval task is what actually shows up in the approver's My Inbox. It needs a Task Details section (subject, priority) and a Recipients section (who gets the task). 

  1. Open the ApprovalForm task and set the Subject to something dynamic, like "Invoice Approval for {Invoice Number}", so each task is identifiable at a glance. 
  1. Under Recipients, add the approver's email address (or a group) — this determines whose inbox the task lands in. 
  1. Set the Due Date type to Reference Date and bind it to the invoice's Due Date field. 

 

 

ApprovalForm task configuration — subject, recipients, and due date settings. 

Next, build the form UI itself. Rather than designing it from scratch, base it on the same layout as InvoiceFormSubmit, but make every field read-only — the approver should see the invoice clearly without being able to edit it. 

  1. Bind each field on the approval form to the corresponding output from InvoiceFormSubmit: Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Supplier, Bill To, Currency, Purchase Order, and the Products Details list. 
  1. Bind Subtotal, Tax Amount, Total Amount, Name, and Email in the same way. 

 

 

Mapping InvoiceFormSubmit output fields into the ApprovalForm's inputs. 

 

 

Continuing the input mapping — Products Details bound as a list, plus Purchase Order, Subtotal, and Tax Amount. 

This mapping is what lets the approver see the exact invoice that was submitted, without any manual re-entry. 

Step 4: Configure the Approval Email 

Once a decision is made, the requester (or a stakeholder) should be notified automatically. 

  1. Add a Send Mail step on the Approve branch. 
  1. Set the To field by binding it to the Email field captured on the original form. 
  1. Set a dynamic Subject, such as "Invoice approval for Invoice No. {Invoice Number}". 
  1. In the Mail Body, greet the requester by name and include the key invoice details — Invoice Number, Supplier, Total Amount, and Currency — followed by a confirmation line. 

 

 

Building the approval email — binding process variables directly into the mail body. 

The same pattern applies to the Send Rejection Mail step on the Reject branch, just with different messaging. 

Step 5: Set Up the Mail Destination 

For BPA to actually send emails, it needs an outbound mail server configured as a Destination in your BTP subaccount — this is what BPA uses as the sender. 

Reference SAP Help Portal: Configure an SMTP Mail Destination-    
https://help.sap.com/docs/intelligent-robotic-process-automation/factory-user-guide/configure-smtp-mail-destination 

  1. In your BTP Cockpit, go to Connectivity > Destinations and create a new destination named sap_process_automation_mail (BPA looks for this name specifically). 
  1. Set Type to MAIL, Proxy Type to Internet, and Authentication to Basic Authentication with your mail account's credentials. 

 

 

The mail destination's main properties and authentication. 

  1. Add the required additional properties for an SMTP mail server: transport protocol, SMTP host and port, the from address, and the relevant TLS/SSL flags. 

 

 

Additional SMTP properties on the mail destination — host, port, TLS settings, and sender address. 

Once saved, this destination becomes the sender identity for every Send Mail step in the process. 

Step 6: Deploy and Test the Full Flow 

With everything wired up, it's time to release and deploy the project, then run it end to end. 

  1. Release and deploy the project. Copy the Form Link for InvoiceFormSubmit — this is the URL used to submit a new invoice. 
  1. Open the link and fill in a sample invoice — line items, totals, and a contact email — then hit Submit. 

 

 

Submitting a sample invoice through the InvoiceFormSubmit form. 

  1. Since the Total Amount exceeds 4000, the process routes to manual approval. Log in to My Inbox — the task appears with the invoice details already populated. 

 

 

The approval task in My Inbox, showing the read-only invoice details and Approve / Reject buttons. 

  1. Click Approve. The process resumes down the Approve branch and fires the Send Mail step. 
  1. Check the recipient's inbox — the approval email arrives with the invoice summary. 

 The approval email received in Gmail, confirming the invoice was approved. 

Wrapping Up 

🎉 That completes a full invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation — from form submission, through conditional routing and human approval, to automated email notification. 

What I found useful in this POC was how easily the individual BPA components fit together. The form collects the data, the condition applies the business rule, the approval form handles the human decision, and the email step communicates the result. Even though the example uses a simple invoice threshold, the same pattern can be extended to many other approval scenarios. 

In the next post, we'll look at combining this same approval pattern with SAP Document Information Extraction, so invoice data doesn't need to be entered manually at all — it gets extracted directly from an uploaded PDF.

entry.title: How We Built a Unified, AI-Powered Monitoring Solution for the SAP Landscape Using SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

In most organizations running SAP, monitoring doesn't live in one place. There's one screen for SAP Integration Suite flows, another for SAP SuccessFactors Integration Center, a third for scheduled jobs, and yet another for data replication status. During my work across SAP SuccessFactors and integration landscapes, I've repeatedly seen support and integration teams jump between four or five different consoles just to answer a simple question: “is everything running fine today?”

The real cost isn't just the inconvenience. It's the delay. A failed integration flow or a discarded replication record can sit unnoticed for hours because nobody was looking at that particular screen at that particular time. By the time someone does notice, the failure has often already affected downstream processes, payroll runs, or employee data accuracy.

Adding more dashboards isn't the answer either. What teams actually need is one place that pulls every SAP system's monitoring data together, tells them clearly what's failing and why, and lets them act on it immediately rather than after the fact. That's the problem we set out to solve.

Our Approach

To address this, we built One Monitoring Solution for SAP SuccessFactors HCM, a centralized monitoring extension on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) using the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) and SAPUI5.

While designing the solution, the goal was simple: don't just aggregate logs, make sense of them. Instead of dumping every system's raw output into one long table and leaving the interpretation to the user, the solution consolidates monitoring data from SAP Integration Suite, SAP SuccessFactors HCM, SAP S/4HANA, SAP ERP, and EC Payroll into one dashboard, visualizes it through built-in analytics, and uses AI to explain why something failed rather than just flagging that it did.

What mattered most during development was closing the loop. A monitoring tool that only shows failures still leaves someone to notice them. So the solution goes a step further: when something fails, it analyzes the error automatically and emails the responsible team, without anyone needing to be watching a screen at all. And when a team wants to dig deeper, a built-in AI Assistant lets them simply ask about failures, trends, or specific modules in plain language.

See One Monitoring Solution in Action

Before going into the key features and technical architecture, here is a short demonstration of the solution showing the unified monitoring dashboard, analytics, AI-powered error analysis, and AI Assistant.

Watch the short video:  One Monitoring Solution for SAP SuccessFactors HCM | AI-Powered SAP Monitoring

 

Key Features and Benefits

1. Unified Monitoring Dashboard

The dashboard brings every connected SAP system into one view: SAP SuccessFactors HCM, SAP Integration Suite, EC Payroll, SAP S/4HANA, and SAP ERP. At a glance, it shows Total Logs, Completed, Failed, and Running counts, along with a source-level breakdown for Integration Suite, SF Scheduled Jobs, SF Integration Center, and SF Data Replication. There's no need to open five different systems to check five different statuses.

 

Fig: One Monitoring Solution landing page and dashboard

2. Monitoring Analytics and Insights

Raw counts only tell part of the story, so the solution includes a built-in analytics view: a Status Distribution chart, a Source Distribution chart, a Logs Trend by Day chart, and a Top Recurring Errors chart. This makes it easy to spot patterns, for example, a specific integration flow failing repeatedly, or a spike in discarded records on a particular day, without manually scanning through hundreds of log rows.

3. Centralized Monitoring Logs

Every monitored flow, job, and replication record across the SAP landscape lands in a single, consolidated table showing Source, Name/Flow, ID/GUID, Status, Start Time, End Time, and Error Message. Teams no longer need to remember which system's console has which log.

 

Fig: All Monitoring Logs, with AI Analysis available on failed and discarded records

4. Advanced Filtering and Search

The logs table can be filtered by source, status, and a custom date range, or searched by flow name directly. This makes it possible to answer specific operational questions in seconds, such as “show me every completed SF Scheduled Job in the last few weeks,” instead of scrolling through unrelated records to find them.

 

Fig: Monitoring logs filtered by source, status, and date range

5. AI-Powered Error Analysis

This is where the solution moves beyond simple log aggregation. For any failed or discarded record, a one-click AI Analysis action calls an AI-based analysis service to interpret the technical error message and return a plain-language explanation of the likely root cause. This removes a lot of the guesswork that usually falls on whoever happens to be on call.

 

Fig: AI Assistant analyzing a failed monitoring record and explaining the root cause 

6. AI Assistant for Monitoring Data

Alongside the logs view, a conversational AI Assistant lets teams ask natural-language questions about monitoring data, such as failures, trends, or specific modules, and get instant answers grounded in live data. Quick-access prompts like “What are today's top errors?”, “Summarize failed jobs,” and “Explain SF Data Replication issues” make it easy to get an answer without building a filter manually.

 

 Fig: Built-in AI Assistant answering questions about monitoring data

7. Workflow Monitoring and Tracking :

Beyond integration and job logs, the solution also tracks end-to-end workflow activity across HRIS and generic object processes. A dedicated dashboard shows total workflows, completed, cancelled, pending, rejected, and sent-back counts, alongside status and module distribution charts, a daily trend view, and average completion percentage by module. Each workflow can be traced down to a step-by-step activity timeline, showing who processed each step, what action was taken, and when. 

 

 Fig: Workflow logs with real-time progress tracking

 

 Fig: Workflow Steps & Activity popup 

8. Automated Email Notifications

Once a failure is detected and analyzed, the solution doesn't wait for someone to check the dashboard. It automatically sends an email notification to the responsible team containing the AI-generated root cause explanation, so the right people know about an issue the moment it happens rather than whenever they next log in.

9. Secure SAP Integration

Underneath all of this, the solution connects securely to every source system using OAuth-secured OData APIs, SAP Destination Service, and the SAP BTP runtime. All data retrieval, analysis, and logging happens within the boundaries of SAP BTP, with SAP Identity Authentication Service handling authentication throughout.

Business Value

This solution delivers value on both the operational and the risk side of monitoring.

  • It gives teams complete visibility into SAP landscape health from a single screen, instead of switching between multiple system-specific consoles.
  • It shortens the time between a failure occurring and a team becoming aware of it, through automated, AI-driven alerts rather than manual checking.
  • It reduces the technical expertise required for first-level triage, since the AI analysis explains the likely root cause rather than just surfacing a raw stack trace.
  • It cuts down on repetitive manual log-checking, freeing up time for actual issue resolution instead of issue discovery.
  • It's built to scale, so additional SAP or non-SAP systems can be brought into the same monitoring view as the landscape grows.

Conclusion

Monitoring a single SAP system is manageable. Monitoring five of them, each with its own console, its own login, and its own way of reporting failures, is where things start slipping through the cracks.

One Monitoring Solution for SAP SuccessFactors HCM was built to close that gap: one dashboard, built-in analytics, AI-powered root cause analysis, a conversational AI Assistant, and automated alerts, all covering the full breadth of a hybrid SAP landscape.

From my own experience supporting SAP integration and SuccessFactors environments, the biggest win isn't the dashboard itself; it's what teams stop having to do manually once it's in place. Instead of checking four consoles every morning and manually reading stack traces when something breaks, teams get a single, AI-assisted view of what's happening and what needs attention.

Ultimately, this isn't just about consolidating screens. It's about giving teams back the time they used to spend hunting for problems, so they can spend it solving them instead.

entry.title: Your ABAP backlog is not a capacity problem. We gave the AI toolchain to consultants, not developers
entry.content:
Two weeks later, for the first time in the company's history, we did not have enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue.

For years we had the same problem every SAP shop has. Not enough ABAP capacity. A queue of business requirements that never got shorter. Recruitment that never quite closed the gap, because senior ABAP people are scarce and expensive, and because the mid-level people you can actually hire need supervision from the senior people you could not hire.

We worked on this for a long time, and we worked on it hard. We tried a great deal, and for most of that time we treated it as a productivity problem, which is what everyone does. Make the developers faster. Give them better completion, better refactoring, better generation. Every one of those attempts produced something real, and none of them made the queue shorter.

Eventually we stopped and asked a different question: who is actually waiting?

The answer was not the developer. The developer was busy. The thing that was waiting was the requirement, and it was waiting in the gap between the person who understood it and the person who could implement it.

Reaching that conclusion took far longer than implementing it. Once we accepted it, we moved the tooling across that gap and gave it to the consultants.

That took two weeks. Nothing about our developers changed in those two weeks. Same people, same skills, same system. What changed was who started the work, and how much context survived before it started.

This article describes what we built, what it cost us to get there, what it does not do, and what we measured.

The bottleneck was never typing speed

Consider what happens to an ordinary custom requirement in an ordinary SAP project.

A business user describes what they need to a functional consultant. The consultant understands it, because the consultant sits close to the business and knows how this particular company has configured and extended SAP. The consultant writes it down. That document goes to a developer, who knows the system deeply but was not in the room and does not carry the business context. Meetings follow. The developer builds something. The consultant tests it, finds the three things the specification did not quite say, and explains again. Another round. Then another.

None of that is anybody's fault. It is a structural property of how the work is divided. Every hop across that boundary loses fidelity, and the loss is recovered through iteration, which is expensive and slow.

The second structural problem is testing. A developer often cannot meaningfully test what they built, because a real test needs business data, a business process and a judgement about whether the result is right. That judgement lives with the consultant. So the developer builds, hands over, waits, and then context-switches back days later to fix it.

Neither problem is solved by making the developer type faster. Both are solved by removing the hop.

What the rest of the industry is building right now

There is a lot of good work happening on AI-assisted ABAP development, and much of it is built on top of the development environment. Giving an AI assistant proper structured context about ABAP objects, instead of leaving it to infer from code completion, is a real improvement and the people doing it are doing it well.

We are not competing with that. We have a different goal, and one of our working principles is that we do not rebuild what the market already provides. Because everything here speaks MCP, those tools and ours can sit in the same landscape and serve the same consultant.

The difference is the audience. Tooling built on top of the development environment naturally serves the person who lives in the development environment. That improves the developer's part of the process. Our finding, after trying hard to improve exactly that part, is that the developer's part of the process was not the constraint.

The change we made

We built the toolchain for the consultant.

That is a different design problem. A consultant needs more than code generation. To take a requirement from a business user all the way to something testable, a consultant needs:

  • Knowledge of how this company has already built things, so the new thing is consistent with the old ones
  • Business data and transactions, so the result can be tested immediately against reality
  • Development tools, so the specification can become code
  • The company's own rules, so the code that comes out is the code this company would have written

Give a consultant those four things through an AI agent and something changes in the economics. The consultant does not translate the requirement to a developer. The consultant works the requirement into a functional specification, then a technical specification, then ABAP code, then tests it with real data, in one continuous session, while still holding the business context that made them the right person to understand it in the first place.

The magic is not the code generation. Code generation is a commodity. The magic is that a person who understands the requirement never has to hand it to someone who does not.

What the setup looks like

 Figure 1. The consultant works in one place. Four logical MCP servers supply knowledge, data, governance and tooling; the three platform-side ones can be deployed separately or combined. The interactive tier is exchangeable.

Four logical MCP servers, two backends, one place for the consultant to work. How they are deployed is a configuration choice, covered at the end of this section.

1. An MCP server published from the ABAP system itself

This is the piece that most differentiates the setup, so it is worth being precise about it.

The MCP server runs in the ABAP stack and is published through SICF. The reason is a different goal, not a different opinion about existing tooling. What this process needs from the ABAP system is business data, transactional actions and a handful of development tools, all provisioned under control. That is a provisioning problem, and the ABAP stack is where it gets solved.

None of that is a judgement about ADT. ADT is a development environment and it is very good at being one. This setup simply does not need that power to do its job, so we did not build toward it. If a customer wants it, the community MCP servers built on top of ADT connect alongside ours and serve the same consultant. We would far rather that happened than spend our time rebuilding something the market already provides and already does well.

Because it is published from the ABAP system, SAP's own authentication and authorization apply to every single call. There is no parallel permission model to maintain and no service user quietly holding more authority than the person using it. If a consultant is not authorized to see a plant, the agent does not see that plant either.

Provisioning is explicit and object by object. You nominate which tables, views and CDS views are exposed. You nominate which ABAP classes act as tools. There is a kill switch at the server.

Through it, the consultant's agent gets:

  • Business data: selected tables, views and CDS views
  • Business transactions: ABAP classes exposed as callable tools, so the agent can create and change documents the same way a user would
  • Development tools: read source code, read object metadata, read short dumps, inspect transports

That last group is what makes the specification honest. The agent does not recall what a table looks like. It reads it.

 Figure 2. The MCP server is a standard ICF service. Authentication and authorization are SAP's, not a parallel model.

 Figure 3. What the consultant actually sees: business transactions, nominated data sources and development tools in one list.

2. An MCP server for ABAP Code Intelligence

Most companies cannot answer a simple question about their own custom code: have we already built something like this?

Background AI agents on the Skybuffer AI platform read the entire custom estate out of the SAP backend and document it automatically. The documentation is vectorized immediately, which turns it into something the consultant's agent can search semantically during a task.

The effect is not mainly documentation for humans. It is that every new development starts with the question "what already exists here" answered. That raises integrity of the custom code base, drives reuse instead of reinvention, and surfaces harmonization and modernization candidates.

 Figure 4. Custom code is read, documented and vectorized continuously, so reuse is the default rather than an accident.

3. An MCP server for the company's development rules

Naming conventions. In-house ABAP standards. Clean ABAP. Clean core principles. Specification templates. The development contract that says what a functional specification must contain before it is allowed to become a technical specification.

These are usually in a wiki that nobody opens. Here they are in the task context, at the moment the decision is being made, which is the only moment they matter.

4. An MCP server for tooling

ABAP Cleaner and other post-processors, applied to generated code before a human looks at it.

This is deliberately an open ecosystem. SAP standard MCP servers, community ones, ADT-based servers for the developers who want them: they all connect alongside. Nothing here is exclusive, and nothing here duplicates something that already exists on the market.

A note on how these are deployed. The four above are a logical grouping rather than a required topology. The first is necessarily its own server, because it lives in the ABAP stack. The three provisioned from the Skybuffer AI platform can run as three servers or be combined into one, and which tools each exposes is configured per customer. We run ours combined, because our internal development process is a single process; a customer whose code standards and tooling sit with different owners may well want them apart. The configuration follows the customer's development process rather than the other way round.

 Figure 5. Platform-side tooling, here deployed as a single combined MCP server: search the documented estate, apply in-house rules, clean the generated code.

The orchestration layer

The MCP servers are the asset. The orchestration unit connects to them and can be exchanged. Which model sits there is a current engineering choice, and we cover the reasoning below.

Where the data lives, and who can support it

In serious conversations about this, two questions arrive before the technical ones. They deserve direct answers.

Your data stays yours, in your own infrastructure

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise. Either way it is the customer's landscape. The documented custom code, the vector store built from it, the in-house rule base and the configuration of the development process all sit inside the customer's infrastructure and belong to the customer.

The MCP server that exposes business data runs inside the ABAP stack itself. Data is not copied out to a platform so that an agent can reach it. It is read in place, per call, under the requesting user's own SAP authorizations. Nothing is staged, replicated or synchronised into a third-party store to make any of this work.

This is a consequence of the architecture rather than a policy bolted on top of it. There is no separate data layer to govern, because there is no separate copy of the data.

Built on SAP technologies, so anyone who supports SAP can support this

The solution is developed using SAP technologies only. It is an ABAP add-on plus a BTP or HANA application. It is not a black box with a proprietary runtime or a specialist skill set attached to it.

That has a consequence people tend to underestimate at purchase time and feel sharply two years later: your own internal SAP team can support it, and so can any SAP partner you already work with. You are not introducing a component into your landscape that only one vendor is able to touch, and you are not making your ABAP estate dependent on a skill set your team does not have and cannot hire.

No lock-in to a closed architecture

Nothing here requires a particular cloud offering. The platform deploys where you already run SAP. The MCP layer is an open protocol, which is why customers can add SAP standard or community MCP servers next to ours, and why the orchestration unit can be exchanged without rebuilding anything underneath it.

The thing you are investing in is your own documented custom estate, your own rule base and your own provisioned tool set. Those stay yours regardless of what you decide to run on top of them.

Two model tiers, chosen for two different jobs

There is no single "the AI" in this architecture. There are two tiers doing unrelated work, and they are not staffed by the same model for good reasons.

The background tier runs on the customer's own model, usually self-hosted. The agents that read the entire custom code estate, document it and vectorize it are doing bulk work where latency is not a KPI anyone is optimizing. If a full pass takes a weekend, nothing is harmed. That makes them a natural fit for a self-hosted LLM inside the customer's landscape, which is what most customers choose. Some run them on a single small GPU unit; an NVIDIA DGX Spark class device is enough for this workload.

This tier matters most for the data question, because this is the tier that touches everything. Every custom object, every piece of business logic, the complete estate. That entire pass happens inside the customer's infrastructure, on a model the customer selected, and the resulting knowledge base stays there.

The interactive tier is where the consultant works, and today we run Opus 5 Max there. That choice is specific rather than incidental, and the reason is not "it writes nice code."

The constraint is discipline under a governed process. Our development contract requires the agent to read the framework contract from live implementations rather than recall it, to verify every table and field against the live dictionary, and to stop when something cannot be verified. A model that shortcuts tool calls to produce a faster, more complete-looking answer breaks that contract no matter how good the templates are.

So what we need from the interactive model is narrower than general capability. It has to keep calling tools, as many times as the task actually requires, until the context is genuinely complete. And it has to hold and reason over the very large runtime context that results from doing so. As of today, that combination is what Opus 5 Max does well, and it is why the generated ABAP comes out integrated with the existing custom development and accurate to the customer's backend release rather than to a plausible average of the internet.

One honest boundary

The interactive tier is the single component that can sit outside the landscape. What crosses is the context assembled for one task, not the estate. We would rather state that plainly than let a reader discover it.

The architecture is built so that this position is exchangeable, which is the practical answer for anyone whose isolation requirements are absolute: point the interactive tier at a self-hosted model as well. Nothing underneath changes, because the MCP servers, the knowledge base and the governance do not care what is connected to them. The honest trade-off is that today you will give up some code quality by doing so, and how much depends on how well the model you choose sustains long tool-calling chains.

Why this does not just produce confident nonsense

This is the first question every experienced SAP person asks, and they are right to ask it.

The answer is not "the model is good." The answer is that the process forbids guessing, and the tooling makes not guessing cheaper than guessing.

A worked example from our own governed pipeline. The agent was building a new MCP tool and needed the framework contract: superclass, method signatures, error mechanism. The rule in our development contract is that it must read this from existing implementations, never recall it. So it read five objects in a fixed order.

Two things came out of that which no amount of model quality would have produced:

First, the metadata-reading tool reports a blank superclass for classes that genuinely do inherit. Reading the source instead showed the real inheritance. An agent working from metadata alone would have generated a structurally wrong class that implemented interfaces directly instead of inheriting from the framework base. It would have looked plausible and failed on activation.

Second, and more instructive: the specification needed two SAP authorization objects. The agent could not verify them. The system exposes no metadata path for authorization objects, and no existing tool in our library performed a comparable check that could be read as precedent. A generative tool optimizing for a complete-looking answer would have filled in the two most likely names.

It did not. It recorded them as unverified, raised a blocking open question with a named owner, isolated the two values in the code as single-point-of-change constants, and stated that the object must not be transported beyond development until a human confirms them.

That is the difference between a demo and a development process. The valuable output is not only the code. It is the code plus an explicit, honest list of what is still unknown.

What a task actually looks like

  1. The consultant brings a business requirement, usually straight from the conversation with the user.
  2. The agent loads the governed context: templates, in-house rules, and a semantic search of what already exists in the custom estate.
  3. Together they produce a functional specification. The agent verifies every table and field it names against the live system as it writes.
  4. The functional specification becomes a technical specification, with the framework contract read from real implementations rather than recalled.
  5. Code is generated from the technical specification, then run through ABAP Cleaner.
  6. The consultant tests it immediately, using the business transactions and data exposed through the same MCP server, without leaving the session or booking anyone's time.
  7. Unknowns that could not be resolved are listed as open questions with owners. Blocking ones stop the object from moving forward.

Steps 3 through 6 used to be a multi-week loop involving at least two people and several meetings.

What we measured

Inside our own company, within the first weeks:

  • About 40% reduction in the ABAP development capacity we needed. This is not a ceiling. We are still optimizing.
  • For the first time ever, not enough tasks to fill the ABAP developer queue — an inversion of the constraint we had been fighting for years.
  • Consultants completing volumes of work in one to two weeks that previously took far longer.

With a customer already running the new process, the effect showed up almost immediately. These are results from the first weeks of adoption, not from a mature steady state:

  • A backlog of critical business requirements cleared, after sitting unaddressed
  • Most projects delivered to UAT within one month
  • Up to 90% savings per project
  • $0.1M–$0.2M USD returned each week

The number the customer cared about most was none of those. It was that the queue of business requirements shrank. Business users stopped hearing "that is in the backlog" as the standard answer to a reasonable request.

That speed of return is the part worth pausing on. This is not a transformation programme that pays back over two years. The mechanism is simply that work stops waiting in a handoff, so the effect appears as soon as the first requirements go through the new path.

Set against the roughly 10% cost saving that classic developer-focused automation typically delivers, the difference is not incremental. It comes from moving the work, not from speeding up the typing.

The honest part

A few things we would want to know if we were reading this rather than writing it.

The consultant's job gets harder, not easier. This surprised us. Consultants were exhausted by the old cycle of meetings, explanation, testing and re-explanation, and they were glad to see it go. But spending the day in dialogue with a very knowledgeable agent is intense work. It demands more decisions per hour than the old process did. Our consultants report being happier, and they also report being more tired. Plan for that.

You still need ABAP developers. Complex architecture, performance work at scale, framework-level changes, and review of anything sensitive still need senior ABAP judgement. What changes is the ratio, and what those developers spend their day on. We reduced capacity by 40%; we did not reduce it to zero, and we would not want to.

This requires governance to exist before it can be automated. If your naming conventions, development standards and specification templates are informal or absent, the agent has nothing to be grounded in and you will get plausible, inconsistent output. The uncomfortable prerequisite is writing your rules down.

The first weeks are not representative. Early gains come partly from clearing a backlog that had accumulated. The steady-state number is lower than the first-month number. We are still measuring ours.

Where to start

You do not have to do all of this at once, and you should not.

  1. Make your custom estate legible. Run automated documentation over existing custom code and vectorize it. This has standalone value even if you stop here, because it answers "what do we already have" for every future project.
  2. Publish a narrow MCP server from your ABAP system. Start read-only, with a small set of nominated tables and development tools. SAP authorization does the access control, so the blast radius is whatever you provision.
  3. Write down the rules. Naming conventions, in-house standards, and one governed specification template. Put them where the agent reads them.
  4. Pick one consultant and one real requirement. Not a pilot with a toy scope. A real thing somebody is waiting for.
  5. Add transactional tools only once reading is solid, so the consultant can test in the same session.

Closing

We spent a long time, and a great deal of effort, trying to make developers faster before we accepted that we were optimizing the wrong side of the handoff. That conclusion was harder to reach than it looks written down, and we would not have believed it without running it on ourselves first.

The result is not that ABAP developers are unnecessary. It is that a large share of custom development does not need to cross the boundary between the person who understands the requirement and the person who implements it. When it does not have to cross, it does not have to wait.

If your business users are being told their requirements are in the queue, the queue is probably not a capacity problem. It is probably a translation problem.

The Skybuffer AI platform runs on SAP BTP or on SAP HANA on premise, inside the customer's own landscape, and is built entirely on SAP technologies, so an internal SAP team or any SAP partner can support it. It is available on SAP Store. It was SAP Certified as Built with SAP Business AI, and was a finalist in the SAP Innovation Awards 2025 as a partner-built product. If you are working on the same problem from the developer side, we would like to compare notes, and we are genuinely interested in where this approach breaks.

entry.title: SAP Document AI: Extracting Information from Documents
entry.content:
Introduction:

Let’s be honest: every business handles a large volume of documents, such as vendor invoices, purchase orders, and payment advices. The key information in these files must eventually be stored in SAP systems.

In my case, I had a real requirement to capture data from PDF and document files and store it for downstream business processing. Without AI, this work is mostly manual: users read each document, identify required fields, and enter them into the system. This approach is slow, repetitive, and prone to errors.

This is where SAP Document AI helps. It automatically reads PDFs and document images, extracts the required information, and returns structured output that can be directly used in business workflows. Instead of spending time on manual data entry, teams can focus on validation and process execution.

In this blog, I will explain how SAP Document AI works, how schema drives extraction, and how this helps solve real-world document processing challenges.

SAP Document AI

SAP Document AI is an end-to-end document processing solution that extracts information from your business documents automatically. Got an invoice as a PDF? Upload it. SAP Document AI reads it, identifies the relevant fields, pulls out the data, and hands it to you in a structured format — ready to be used in your business processes. It handles both structured documents (like invoices with predictable layouts) and unstructured documents (where information could be anywhere on the page).

Supported File Types:
  • JPEG / JPG
  • PDF
  • PNG
  • TIF / TIFF

Whether your vendor sends a scanned PDF or a photo of an invoice — it can handle it.

How Does It Know What to Extract? That's Where Schema Comes In

Here's the thing: every business cares about different data points. Some companies need the tax ID, others don't. Some track payment terms, others skip it. So how does SAP Document AI know what to look for?

What is a Schema?

A schema is essentially a blueprint that describes the structure of your data  what fields you need extracted, what they're called, and what type of data they contain. You have two options: standard and custom schemas. With custom schemas, you
define your own fields and provide specific extraction details. With standard schemas, pre-built configurations are available in the dropdown — no customization needed.

Defining a Schema (Custom)

When you create a schema, you define two categories of fields:

Header Fields — Information that appears once per document:

  • Invoice Number
  • Invoice Date
  • Vendor Name
  • Total Amount

Line Items — Repeating rows of data:

  • Material Description
  • Quantity
  • Unit Price
  • Line Total

For each field, you specify:

PropertyWhat It Means
NameTechnical name of the field (e.g., `invoiceNumber`)
LabelHuman-readable name (e.g., "Invoice Number")
DescriptionWhat this field represents — helps the AI understand context
Data TypeThe type of data expected (string, number, date, etc.)
Setup TypeManual

Note: Don’t forget to activate the schema. If you do not activate it, it will not appear under the document schema list.

Setting Up a Document

Once your schema is ready, you move to the Document configuration. Here you'll find a few options:

Document Type

Choose what kind of document you're working with:

  • Invoice
  • Purchase Advice
  • Purchase Order
  • Custom(for anything else)
Schema

Select which schema to apply — only active schemas appear in the dropdown. This links your document type to the fields you want extracted.

In my implementation, I processed a vendor purchase order (PO_2026-001234).
The system extracted key fields with confidence ranging from 76% to 100%.

Here's what happened next:
• PO_Number (confidence 98%): Directly validated against existing POs
• SHIP-TO_PARTY (confidence 76%): Manually reviewed to extract customer number
• Delivery_Date (confidence 92%): Auto-filled with warning for manual date validation
• Email (confidence 88%): Auto-populated but marked for verification

Here's how it all fits together:

entry.title: Connecting SAP Build Process Automation to a Trial Document AI Instance
entry.content:
Diagnosing a landscape mismatch between BPA and SAP Document AI on trial, and building a reusable extraction flow around it. 

Introduction 

In the first post of this series, we built an invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation, triggered by a manually filled form. The natural next step is to remove that manual step — read the invoice straight from a PDF and feed the extracted data into the same approval process. 

That's exactly where this post started. But before we could get to the approval logic, we ran into a connectivity issue between BPA and SAP Document AI that's specific to trial landscapes. This post covers how we diagnosed it, the workaround that actually gets extraction working, and the one limitation that comes with it. 

The Error 

The first attempt was the obvious one: use BPA's built-in "Add a Document Template" wizard to register a template against our invoice schema. It failed immediately, before any real document was even involved. 

 

 

SAP_IPA_28014 — the Document Information Extraction call fails with a 400 Bad Request, right at the template creation step. 

Swapping the approach and trying the built-in Extract Data (Pre-Trained Model) activity directly against our sample invoice hit the same wall. 

 

 

Extract Data (Pre-Trained Model) configured against a sample invoice PDF. 

What Didn't Work 

Our first instinct was that this was a subscription/entitlement glitch — a stale binding between the BPA and Document AI subscriptions. We re-subscribed both services from scratch a couple of times, on the theory that it would force a fresh landscape mapping. It didn't change anything; the same 400 kept coming back. 

Finding the Actual Cause 

The real answer came from comparing what URL the failing call was actually hitting against what our trial tenant's URL actually is. 

The Test Console error for the built-in activity exposes the full request, including the URL it tried to call: 

 

 

The built-in Extract Data activity was calling https://us10.doc.cloud.sap/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs. 

Then we pulled the actual service key for our SAP Document AI trial instance from the subaccount's Instances and Subscriptions page: 

 

 

SAP Document AI, subscribed under the trial subaccount alongside SAP Build Process Automation. 

 

 

The service key's credentials show the real backend URL: https://us10-trial.doc.cloud.sap — not https://us10.doc.cloud.sap. 

That's the mismatch. SAP Document AI base URLs follow the pattern https://<tenant-id>.<region>.doc.cloud.sap, and trial-tier URLs are distinguished by the -trial substring appearing in both the tenant and regional domain segments — while standard and premium plans map directly to the plain commercial landscape (us10, eu10, etc.). BPA's built-in Extract Data activities are resolving the endpoint from the region alone and dropping that -trial qualifier, so on a trial subaccount they always call a host that doesn't exist for our tenant. That explains the immediate 400, independent of anything about our schema, template, or document. 

The Fix: a Destination-Based Extraction Flow 

Since the built-in activities resolve the URL internally, there's no setting inside them to correct it. The workaround is to stop using those activities altogether and call SAP Document AI through an explicit BTP Destination instead, using a set of reusable Document AI activities that take the destination as a parameter rather than assuming a URL. 

We built this on top of the approach and reusable automation package shared in Using Document AI Premium in SAP Build Process Automation, which packages a set of Document AI activities (extraction, capabilities, clients, schema lookup, job status, and Premium-specific calls) that go through a destination rather than a hardcoded region URL. The project and its GitHub repo are linked from that post. 

  1. Create a Destination in the BTP Cockpit pointing to the correct trial URL — in our case https://us10-trial.doc.cloud.sap/document-information-extraction/v1 — using OAuth2ClientCredentials authentication with the Document AI service key's client ID and secret. 

 

 

The Document_AI destination — Type HTTP, pointing at the correct -trial URL, authenticated via OAuth2ClientCredentials. 

  1. Add the additional properties BPA needs to recognize and use the destination from within a process automation project — these enable it for use as a connector inside BPA and Build Apps. 

 

 

Additional destination properties: sap.processautomation.enabled, BuildApps.Enabled, and related flags set to true.

entry.title: Leveraging Joule Studio for SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
I'm excited to share my first blog, based on my learnings and experience working with Joule Studio. @amrutha_g will be the co-author of this blog.

This blog introduces Joule Studio and demonstrates how SAP SuccessFactors users can create tailored conversational experiences using Actions, Skills, and Agents. Through a practical illustration, readers will learn how to build, test, and deploy AI-powered capabilities that enable users to extract business information by communication through natural language.

  1. Introduction to Joule Studio 
  2. Key Features of Joule Studio 
  3. Prerequisites  
  4. Understanding the Three Building Blocks of Joule Studio 
  5. Action Editor Overview 
  6. Skill Editor Deep Dive 
  7. Agent Editor Overview 
  8. Testing Skills and Agents 
  9. Conclusion

Introduction

Joule Studio is an important component of SAP Build; it's a comprehensive suite of low-code and no-code solutions designed to enhance application development and leverage the power of generative AI.

It let’s us expand Joule's capabilities and knowledge to meet the distinct requirements of the organization.

With Joule embedded in SAP SuccessFactors, Joule Studio serves as a workspace to create and deploy custom capabilities. These can in turn be used within our instance to perform informational/ transactional operations with the help of prompts in human language.

Features

  • Develop new skills for Joule that enable it to perform additional, custom, and pre-determined tasks that supports business processes.
  • Design interactive Joule agents that collaborate with Joule to tackle complex or multi-step tasks efficiently.
  • Manage and deploy advanced versions of skills and Joule agents to promote ongoing enhancements and flexibility.

Let us consider a scenario to understand more:

A user has an Employee ID. Using that, they want to fetch the first name and last name of the employee. Instead of navigating around the SuccessFactors UI and searching for an Employee, the user would like to simply ask Joule.

Prerequisites

  • An active user (developer) license is required to build, test, and deploy your custom Joule skills.
  • Joule should be enabled in the SuccessFactors instance

Building Blocks of Joule Studio

There are mainly 3 - building blocks of Joule Studio:

  1. Actions: An action is SAP's building block that wraps a single API call (or endpoint) - defining its inputs and outputs — so that it can be securely exposed and reused inside a Joule Skill or Agent.
  2. Skills: A skill is part of an advanced AI model and can act on specific operations by leveraging the content of the conversation. It helps in combining various Actions together
  3. Agents: A Joule agent is an independent, multipurpose-tool system that solves complex problems by selecting and executing appropriate tools dynamically. It helps combine various skills together.

Creating any of the above blocks requires a project. A project serves as a comprehensive workspace where we can create and manage various skills and agents related to a particular use case.

Before proceeding, start by creating a new project in Joule Studio.

Refer this Create a Project in Joule Studio, classic edition | SAP Help Portal to create a project.

Action Editor

The Action Editor is the workspace where we can create, modify, and manage actions.

The action editor makes API operations available to actions while also simplifying input and output values. We can also use the editor to test the operation of an action. To obtain reusable action artifacts, release and publish the Actions project to the library.

For this scenario, we would be using the Get Entities from User API

The image below illustrates the Action Editor.

The Actions pane consists of a complete list of all the API actions related to the project.

For each API, we have three tabs available: Input, Output and Test.

  • The Input tab is used to define the parameters required by the API to retrieve the desired data. These input parameters are passed to the API during execution and determine the results returned by the API.

Following are the fields available in the Input tab can be used to customize and refine the output returned by the API call.

  • $top: Specifies the maximum number of records to retrieve. By default, all available records are returned.
  • $skip: Specifies the number of records to skip before returning the results.
  • $count: Returns the total number of records that match the query criteria.
  • $filter: Applies conditions to filter the results based on specific field values.
  • $search: Searches for records that match the specified search value.
  • $orderby: Sorts the results based on one or more selected fields.

For our case, we have added the below condition to the $filter tab. ‘userId’ is the corresponding field for the employee ID.

To know more about the API’s and their fields definitions, you can refer to the SAP documentation below:
About SAP SuccessFactors APIs | SAP Help Portal

  • The Output tab consists of two sections: Header and Body. The Body section displays the fields which would be returned by the API call. Here, we can add or remove fields as needed to customize the output according to the requirements. For our scenario, we have retained the fields below and removed the rest.

  • The Test tab is used to validate and test the API using sample input values before using it into actual skill. It helps ensure that the API returns the expected results and allows us to refine the query parameters as needed. Provide the employee ID in $search field and try testing the API

For more information about the Action Editor, refer to below document from SAP:
Overview of an Action Editor | SAP Help Portal

Skill Editor

The Skill Editor is the workspace used to create, modify, and manage skills in Joule Studio.

Skills can be built using any of the following Activities:

  1. Action: Use one or more actions that have been created and incorporate them into the skill workflow.
  2. Process: Configure the skill to invoke a process created in SAP Build Process Automation.
  3. Automation: Configure the skill to trigger an automation built using SAP Build Process Automation.
  4. Skill: Reuse an existing Joule skill by incorporating it into another skill.
  5. Condition: Add decision-making logic to the skill by defining conditions that control the workflow based on specific criteria.

For more information about the activities, refer here: Add Activities to the Skill | SAP Help Portal

In the example shown below, a skill - EmployeeDetails has been created by incorporating an Action into the skill workflow.

The Trigger tab is where we define the basic details of a skill, including its Name, Identifier, and Description. The Identifier is automatically generated and pre-populated by the system.

The Description plays a significant role in aiding the Joule Assistant to understand the skill's purpose and area of specialization. This will allow Joule to identify and invoke the most relevant skill based on the user's prompt.

The Trigger tab is the place where we also define the input and output parameters for the skill.

  • Skill Inputs are variables that capture the information required from the end user. Ex: empid
  • Skill Outputs are used to store the data returned by the skill upon execution. In this case, we will define the variable of type list, so that it returns all the relevant fields.
    For our case, we will define the output of type list, so that it fetches all the relevant results returned by the API call.  

These parameters serve as the interface through which information is passed in and out of the skill.

Next, we can add an Action to the skill workflow by selecting the + icon. This is the action that was created in the previous step.

Each action consists of three tabs: General, Inputs, and Outputs.

The General tab displays the action name along with the Destination Variable. The destination variable stores the endpoint of the instance through which the information needs to be obtained. This will be created by us.

It allows the skill to access and map the action's output data to the appropriate fields, conditions, or downstream actions.

The Inputs tab is used to map the input variables defined earlier in the skill. These variables are passed to the action to ensure that the API receives the correct input values during execution.

In most cases, input variables are configured within the $filter parameter to retrieve the required data based on specific criteria.

Formulas can also be used to combine multiple input variables, aiding the creation of dynamic and more complex API queries.

In this case, the below expression has been used in the $filter tab. We have mapped userId field in the API definition to our skill Input - empid.

The Outputs tab displays the fields returned by the API call. It allows us to view the data that will be available after the action is executed and identify the output fields that can be used in subsequent steps of the skill workflow.

In the End section, map the skill's output variables to the appropriate fields returned by the action. This ensures that the relevant data retrieved from the API call is exposed as the final output of the skill and can be presented to the user or consumed by downstream processes. For this scenario, we have mapped the API result list to our output variable.

Agent Editor

Agents are created by combining one or more skills and providing detailed instructions that define how those skills should be aligned to perform a particular task.

By combining skills with proper execution logic, agents can interpret user requests, determine the relevant actions to be performed, and delivers the required outcome.

Refer to the below SAP documentation to know more about the Agent Editor

Create a Joule Agent | SAP Help Portal

For our case, we will add the 'EmployeeDetails' skill to the tool and provide instructions as below:

“When a user provides an Employee ID, invoke the EmployeeDetails skill using the supplied Employee ID as input. Retrieve the employee information from the skill response and present the results to the user in a clear and structured format. If the Employee ID is missing, prompt the user to provide it. If no employee record is found, inform the user accordingly.”

Testing the Skill/Agent

Once satisfied with the configuration of the skill or agent, select Test to validate its functionality. During testing, provide the appropriate connection details and endpoints for the SAP SuccessFactors instance to ensure successful execution and accurate results.

The image below shows the Joule Test tab.

The above image shows the testing of our skill.

Here, users can test the skill or agent by entering a prompt in natural, conversational language. Joule analyses the prompt and calls the most appropriate skill or agent to handle the request.

On entering the employee ID, Joule fetches the employee’s details from the instance.

Verify that the system correctly identifies and invokes the desired skill or agent based on the user's input. Once the execution is successful, the response is displayed in the chat interface in a clear and structured format, allowing us to validate both the behavior of the skill and the accuracy of the returned results.

After testing, deploy the project. This ensures that the Agent is ready to be used within the Joule chat in the instance.

Conclusion

The blog helps us to explore Joule Studio, and how it can be leveraged for SuccessFactors. It also explains how Actions, Skills, and Agents can contribute to building these experiences. An Action enables a specific operation, Skills help us combine actions, and Agents can help orchestrate these skills together.

With Joule Studio, the possibilities go beyond what the user can find in the application —they can also change how the user interacts with it.

entry.title: How to Use SAP Document AI in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA): A Step-by-Step Demo
entry.content:
Introduction:

If you already know what SAP Document AI is and want to see a practical integration example, this blog is for you.

For a full functional introduction, read my previous post:  SAP Document AI: Extracting Information from Documents.

In short, SAP Document AI automatically extracts structured information from business documents such as invoices and purchase orders. But knowing how it works in theory is one thing. Getting it to work reliably in a real BPA workflow is another.

In this post, I'll walk you through a practical integration—complete with what went wrong on my first attempt, which document types surprised me, and most importantly, proof that the workflow actually delivers value.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • Access to SAP BTP with the Document AI service enabled.
  • (Optional) Access to SAP Build Process Automation.
  • The necessary roles/permissions to call APIs and manage BPA projects.
Step 1: Get a Bearer Token

To call the Document AI API, you need an OAuth Bearer token.
If you’re using a configured destination in SAP BTP, you can skip this step.

Otherwise, use the following API call to get your token:

return{
    method:'GET',
    url:docurl + '/oauth/token?grant_type=client_credentials',
    responseType : 'JSON',
    resolveBodyOnly: true,
    headers: {
        Authorization: 'Basic ' + <Encoded_clientCredentials>
    },
 }

 

Tip : Encode your client ID and client secret as `client_id:client_secret` in Binary for the Authorization header.
 Step 2: Submit Your Document for Extraction

Now, you need to tell Document AI what kind of document you’re sending and which schema to use.
This is done by setting the right metadata in your request.

let documentOption = {
documentType: "custom", // or "invoice", "purchaseOrder", etc.
schemaName: "SAP_invoice_schema",
headerFields: ["purchaseOrderNumber"],
clientId: "default"
};

let payloadDocAICall = {
method: 'POST',
url: <url> + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs",
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
metadataType: irpa_core.enums.request.metadataType.formData,
headers: {
Authorization: <access_token>
},
metadata: [
{
name: "file",
file: <filePath>,
},
{
name: "options",
value: JSON.stringify(documentOption)
}
],

};
return payloadDocAICall;

 

  • documentType: The type of document (e.g., "invoice", "custom")
  • schemaName: The schema you defined in Document AI

Step 3: Check the Job Status

After submitting your document, you’ll get a job ID.
You need to check the status of this job to see if extraction is complete.

let option = {
method: 'GET',
url: docAiUrl + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs/" + <your_job-id>,
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
headers: {
Authorization: <your_token>,
'Cache-Control': 'no-cache'
}
};
return option;
Step 4: Poll Until the Job is Done

In your BPA workflow, use a forever loop (or a repeat-until loop) to keep checking the job status.

  • If the status is `"DONE"`, exit the loop and process the results.
  • If the status is `"PENDING"` or `"RUNNING"`, wait a few seconds and check again.

This ensures you only move forward once the extraction is complete.

Step 5: Process the Extracted Data

Once your job status is `"DONE"`, you can access the extracted fields in the response and use them in your workflow.

Error Handling
  • Always check for errors in API responses (e.g., invalid token, file not found, extraction failed).
  • If the job status returns `"FAILED"`, log the error and notify the user or take corrective action.
  • Handle timeouts and network issues gracefully by retrying or alerting the user.
Real-World Use Case

Imagine you receive 200 vendor invoices every month:

Phase 1 (Manual Entry):

  • 8% error rate = 16 invoices with mistakes
