  3. Consume structured output automatically
  4. Trigger business actions with minimal human effort

This pattern is especially useful for high-volume document scenarios such as invoice intake and validation.

entry.title: From PDF to Decision: Wiring Extraction Straight into the Invoice Approval Process
entry.content:
Closing the loop — PDFs go in, and depending on the amount, they're auto-approved or routed to a human decision, with no manual form-filling anywhere.

Introduction

This is the third post in the series. In the first post, we built the core approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation, triggered by someone manually filling out an invoice form. In the second, we worked around a trial-landscape connectivity issue and built a reusable automation that reads a PDF and extracts its data using SAP Document AI.

This post connects the two. Instead of extraction stopping at a log message, the extracted invoice data is now passed directly into the approval process as a typed input. Depending on the total amount, the process either auto-approves the invoice and sends a confirmation, or creates an approval task in My Inbox for a human decision — and either way, the outcome is emailed back automatically.

Source Documents

For reference, here are the three synthetic invoices used to test the flow — one under the approval threshold, two above it.

 

 

 

DEMO-INV-1001 (approved manually, $4,730), DEMO-INV-2001 (rejected manually, $7,590), and DEMO-INV-2002 (auto-approved, $3,630 — below the threshold) — the three PDFs run through the pipeline.

Typing the Process Input

To call a process directly from an automation, the process needs a well-defined input shape rather than a set of loose form fields. We formalized this as a Data Type — InvoiceApproval_DT — mirroring the same fields used throughout the series: header fields, contact details, and a nested lineItems list.

 

InvoiceApproval_DT — the structured Data Type that now defines the process's expected input, including the nested lineItems object.

The Approval Form, Read-Only and Decision-Ready

The approval form itself is largely the same as Post 1, bound to the same set of fields — but now typed against InvoiceApproval_DT, and every field is locked read-only, since the approver should review, not edit.

 

ApprovalForm — header and contact fields, all read-only, bound to InvoiceApproval_DT.

 

The rest of the form — line items, totals, and the Approve / Reject buttons that drive the outcome.

The Process Logic: Auto-Approve or Escalate

The process itself now has three exits instead of two. Below the threshold, it auto-approves and emails a confirmation with no human step at all. Above the threshold, it creates the approval task, then branches again on the human decision into an approval or rejection email.

 

The full process, with Process Inputs shown on the right — matching InvoiceApproval_DT field for field, including the lineItems list.

 

The branch condition unchanged from Post 1: TotalAmount is greater than 4000.

On the approval branch, every field on the task is bound straight from the process's own inputs — no re-mapping needed, since the process input shape and the form's expected shape are now the same Data Type.

 

ApprovalForm inputs bound directly to the process's InvoiceApproval variables — BillTo, Currency, Due Date, Email, and the rest.

 

The approval email, built the same way as Post 1 — process variables bound straight into the mail body.

Wiring the Extraction Automation to Call the Process

With the process now accepting a typed input, the automation from Post 2 needed exactly one addition: a call to InvoiceApprovalProcess at the end of each loop iteration, passing the extracted data straight through.

  1. Get File Collection still reads every PDF from the source folder.

 

Get File Collection, pointed at the folder of invoice PDFs.

  1. The For Each loop iterates the collection, tracking currentMember and index.

 

For Each — looping list bound to the file collection output.

  1. DocAI - Extract with Schema runs per file, against the InvoiceApprovalSchema created in the Document AI UI — this is the same destination-based extraction activity built in Post 2, unchanged here.

For the full breakdown of why the built-in extraction activities fail on trial, and how this destination-based activity works around it, see Post 2.

 

DocAI - Extract with Schema — unchanged from the extraction-only version in Post 2.

  1. New in this post: immediately after extraction, InvoiceApprovalProcess is called directly, passing the extractedData output as the invoiceapproval input — this is what actually starts a new process instance per invoice.

 

InvoiceApprovalProcess called from inside the loop — invoiceapproval bound to extractedData.

Deploying and Triggering It (No Local Testing Here)

One thing worth calling out for anyone following along: this flow cannot be run from the local Design Console. A process automation has to be released and deployed before it can be invoked from a Task Automation — there's no way around this for an automation-to-process call, unlike testing the automation's extraction logic in isolation.

  1. Release and deploy the full project. The Overview tab confirms everything shipped together as one deployed version: the form, the data type, the automation, and the process.

 

InvoiceApprovalProject3 — deployed and active, with all four artifacts (ApprovalForm, InvoiceApproval_DT, InvoiceApprovalAutomation, InvoiceApprovalProcess) bundled together.

  1. Since there's no form to submit manually here, we used a Scheduled trigger in Control Tower to invoke InvoiceApprovalAutomation.

 

Editing the Scheduled_01 trigger — set to execute InvoiceApprovalAutomation.

  1. Rather than waiting on the schedule, Control Tower's Run now action on the trigger fires it immediately — handy for testing without needing to wait for the next scheduled window.

 

Triggering an on-demand run of the automation via Run now, instead of waiting for the schedule.

From there, both the automation's job and the process instances it spawns can be watched in Monitoring, under the Build Lobby — Task Automation jobs and Process Automation instances show up as separate, correlated entries, which is useful for tracing a single invoice all the way from extraction through to its final decision.

Watching the Three Outcomes

We ran this against three invoices, each landing on a different branch of the process: one below the threshold (auto-approved with no human step), and two above it (one approved, one rejected in My Inbox).

 

My Inbox — DEMO-INV-1001, above the threshold, approved manually.

 

My Inbox — DEMO-INV-2001, also above the threshold, rejected manually.

Each outcome triggers its own email, matched to what actually happened to that invoice:

 

 

 

DEMO-INV-1001 (approved), DEMO-INV-2001 (rejected), and DEMO-INV-2002 (auto-approved, below the threshold) — each outcome emailed back automatically.

Wrapping Up

With this, the series comes full circle: a PDF dropped into a folder is read, extracted, and routed through the same approval logic from Post 1 — auto-approved outright, or handed to a human in My Inbox — with a confirmation email either way, and no manual data entry at any point.

The one operational note worth remembering if you're building something similar: because the automation calls the process directly rather than through a form trigger, there's no local test shortcut — release, deploy, and trigger it for real (a schedule, an API call, or Run now in Control Tower) is the only way to see the full path end to end.

entry.title: SAP's New API Policy v4.2026: What Every Integration and AI Team Needs to Know
entry.content:
For two decades, the unwritten rule of enterprise SAP landscapes was simple: if an API worked, you used it. Documented or not, sanctioned or not, if it moved data reliably, it became load-bearing infrastructure somewhere in your integration stack. That era just ended.

With API Policy v4.2026, SAP has drawn a hard line around what "acceptable access" looks like — and the line falls in a very different place than most organizations assumed. This isn't a footnote in a release cycle. It's a structural reset of how every integration, every automation, and every AI initiative is allowed to touch SAP systems going forward.

CEO Christian Klein has been careful to frame this as something other than a data grab: "Customer's data is customer's data, and accessing those data, we are not going to charge." Take that at face value if you like — the ownership question isn't really the issue here. The issue is that the roads to that data have been narrowed to one lane, with a toll booth and a checkpoint on it.

The four pillars — and why each one bites

  1. "Published Only" means exactly what it sounds like.
    From now on, only APIs listed on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub carry official support. Everything else — every internal endpoint, every private interface, every API a consultant found three years ago that "just worked" — is now unsupported and can be pulled without warning. If you've never audited your integration landscape against the Hub's published list, do it now, because many organizations are about to discover that a meaningful chunk of their "critical path" integrations were never actually sanctioned.
  2. Controls are no longer optional — they're layered.
    SAP is enforcing specific controls per API — rate limits, quotas, deprecation timelines, ingress/egress caps, bulk-extraction preconditions, security requirements — stacked on top of general controls that apply across the board. The days of a single high-throughput integration quietly running at whatever pace your infrastructure could handle are over.
  3. This is the one that should worry your AI roadmap.
    Buried in the policy is a sentence that undercuts a lot of 2025–2026 AI strategy decks: SAP explicitly prohibits "interaction or integration with (semi-) autonomous or generative AI systems that plan, select, or execute sequences of API calls" — unless it happens through SAP-endorsed architectures. Translate that into plain terms: the AI agent you built to auto-triage purchase orders, the intelligent automation layer orchestrating SAP workflows, the third-party ML platform pulling SAP data for a model — all of it now sits in a restricted zone unless it's routed through SAP's own approved pathways. This is the clause that turns "nice-to-have compliance cleanup" into "emergency architecture review."
  4. And they mean to enforce it.
    SAP now reserves the right to actively monitor usage, throttle requests, suspend access, and terminate it outright for violations — and has closed the obvious workarounds. Intermediary services, custom code, proxies, gateways, impersonation techniques — all explicitly named and explicitly banned. This is not a policy meant to be quietly routed around.

The shift, side by side

Area

Before

Now

API Access

Flexible, undocumented endpoints tolerated

Published APIs on the Business Accelerator Hub only

AI Integration

Largely unrestricted

Prohibited for autonomous/generative AI systems outside endorsed paths

Bulk Data Extraction

Limited oversight

Rate limits, quotas, explicit restrictions

Non-Published APIs

Common in practice

Explicitly prohibited, actively enforced

Monitoring

Passive

Active, with throttling and suspension rights

Also now explicitly off-limits: using SAP APIs for competitive analysis of SAP's own products, enabling any function outside its documented use, anything that creates performance or stability risk, and large-scale scraping or systematic data harvesting.

Reading between the lines: this is "Clean Core," enforced by contract

SAP has talked about Clean Core for years as an architectural philosophy. This policy is what happens when a philosophy gets teeth. The stated goals — protecting system health, clearing the path for upgrades, standardizing security, and funneling traffic through the Business Technology Platform (BTP) — aren't new. What's new is that they're no longer aspirational guidance; they're enforceable terms, backed by monitoring infrastructure that can throttle or cut you off. Klein's own words make the intent unambiguous: "When there is mass data requests or millions of calls coming towards an API, we need to start throttling those APIs."

Read plainly, this is SAP consolidating control over its own ecosystem's edges — and BTP is the toll road everyone gets funneled onto.

Where the damage concentrates

Not every team feels this equally. The risk map breaks down like this:

  • Critical — Integration debt. Any existing connection built on an undocumented API needs an immediate audit. This is the fire that needs putting out first.
  • Critical — AI strategy. Generative AI and automation initiatives built around direct, autonomous API orchestration may need to be redesigned from the ground up.
  • High — Data warehouse/lake pipelines. Bulk replication strategies now hit new bottlenecks.
  • High — Partner dependencies. Third-party tools that relied on flexible access may lose functionality without warning.
  • Medium — Analytics and reporting. High-frequency extraction patterns are affected, though generally less existentially than the categories above.

The compliant map forward

SAP hasn't left teams with nowhere to go — but the endorsed paths are narrower and more prescriptive than what many organizations are used to.

For data integration: Business Accelerator Hub APIs remain the baseline. Datasphere and Integration Suite are SAP-endorsed for federation and process integration. Custom ABAP is still permitted in private cloud and on-prem environments. And notably, RFC (Remote Function Call) is explicitly unaffected — for high-volume data access, it remains a genuinely stable option while everything else gets rebuilt around it.

For AI initiatives: SAP Business AI and the Joule assistant are the native, endorsed routes. BTP AI Services is the approved platform layer. Direct API access by third-party AI tools, by contrast, is now restricted — which means a lot of best-of-breed AI tooling built outside SAP's walls just lost its most direct line into SAP data.

What to actually do, starting now

This isn't a "read and file away" policy — it has a clock on it.

Days 0–30:

  • Run a full API inventory audit across every integration
  • Classify each as Published vs. Non-Published against the Business Accelerator Hub
  • Flag every AI or automation dependency specifically
  • Quantify business impact for each non-compliant connection

Days 30–90:

  • Push every third-party vendor for their compliance status and roadmap toward SAP-endorsed alternatives
  • Begin architecture planning around BTP, Datasphere, and Integration Suite
  • Design migration paths for the integrations that matter most

Days 90–180:

  • Migrate non-compliant integrations to Published APIs
  • Redesign AI initiatives through approved channels
  • Rebuild data extraction strategy around the new constraints

One safeguard worth knowing: SAP has stated the policy doesn't override legal obligations around data portability, switching rights, or legally mandated record retention — that door stays open regardless of what else changes.

The takeaway

This policy isn't a minor terms update to skim past. It's SAP telling the ecosystem, in contractual language, exactly where the boundaries of "supported" now sit — and those boundaries have moved a lot closer in than most integration and AI roadmaps assumed. Only published APIs are supported now. AI and automation initiatives need SAP-endorsed pathways or they're out of bounds. Bulk extraction is rate-limited and watched. Non-compliance has real, enforced consequences. And RFC remains the one steady bridge that didn't move.

The organizations that come out ahead here aren't the ones hoping enforcement stays lax — they're the ones auditing now, migrating deliberately, and treating Clean Core as the contractual reality it's just become.

entry.title: SAP Joule for Developers: End of the Promotional Period and The Path Forward
entry.content:
SAP Joule for Developers, which brought generative AI capabilities into SAP Build and ABAP at no additional cost during its initial promotional period, is ending on September 30th, 2026.  We are extending the promo offer for SAP Build features to December 31st, 2026, and this post explains exactly what that means for you, what happens to each capability you may be using today, and what your path forward looks like after December 31st, 2026. 

We know changes like this require planning, and we want to give you as much clarity as possible, well in advance, so you can make informed decisions for your team and your projects. 

What Does This Mean for You? 

If you are using SAP Build generative AI capabilities today — SAP Build Process Automation generative AI features or Joule Studio, classic edition generative AI features — you retain full access through December 31, 2026. AI chat in SAP Build Code is already rolled out in Business Application Studio and will continue beyond December 31, 2026. SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities will be commercially available starting October 1, 2026, outside the promotion (previously announced here). 

SAP Build continues as a customer-managed solution development platform for extending SAP applications. What is changing is the commercial structure behind certain AI capabilities that were offered on a promotional basis, and the transition of the SAP Joule for Developers brand that will only be associated with ABAP AI capabilities as we move into 2027. 

Why Are We Making This Change? 

SAP Joule for Developers promotional period was designed to give customers hands-on experience with generative AI in SAP Build without an immediate commercial commitment. That exploration phase has provided real-world signals on what delivers value. Based on customer feedback, we made deliberate decisions for each capability.  Where usage and value are clear, we are moving capabilities into supported commercial models; where strategic alternatives exist to deliver better customer value, we are directing investment accordingly. 

What Happens to Each Capability?

ABAP AI — Continues under commercial licensing 

As announced in May 2026, ABAP AI moves to consumption-based pricing (PUPM model) effective October 1, 2026. If you are currently using ABAP AI under SAP Joule for Developers promotional access, SAP will contact you before the transition date with licensing details. More details available here. 

Action required: Plan for a licensing transition before October 1, 2026. 

AI assistance in SAP Build Code — Already Available in Business Application Studio 

AI Chat in SAP Build Code has already been rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) for those using build-code (SAP Build Code) or build-default (SAP Build Developer) plans. This will remain available beyond December 31, 2026. No action is required from customers; your AI coding assistance experience is uninterrupted and enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 

SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

SAP Build customers using generative AI features in SAP Build Process Automation — including process generation, decision generation, form generation, script generation, and summarization — can continue using those features until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Your existing automations, processes, and decisions built in SAP Build Process Automation are unaffected. This transition impacts only the ability to use AI while authoring new content, not your existing artifacts.

Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

Customers using Joule Studio, classic edition can continue using its generative AI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test modes until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using Joule Studio, classic edition, but without generative AI support. This specifically and only refers to the generative AI support during design time. You can begin exploring the new Joule Studio and its agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Frequently Asked Questions 

Is SAP Build being deprecated? 

No. SAP Build continues as a customer managed application development platform for extending SAP applications, automations and digital workspaces. 

Do my existing SAP Build projects, automations, and code get affected? 

No. Your built artifacts are fully intact. Only AI-assisted authoring capabilities are affected by this transition. 

Can I keep using SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features? 

Yes — GenAI features continue up to December 31, 2026. After this time, Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test mode will be removed. SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features such as artifact (process, form, data type, decision) creation with natural language will be removed. These GenAI features refer specifically and only to the generative AI support during design time.

What happens after December 31, 2026 for SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI? 

For SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using these products without generative AI support after December 31, 2026. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

What about the AI assistance in SAP Build Code? 

AI Chat is already rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) and continues beyond December 31, 2026. No action needed. 

Will ABAP AI Capabilities still be available after the promotional period ends? 

Yes — ABAP AI capabilities moves to the Per User Per Month (PUPM) commercial license from October 1, 2026. ABAP Development Tools remain free; only the AI capabilities require licensing. 

What should I do right now? 

If you use ABAP AI, engage your SAP account manager to plan the licensing transition before October 1, 2026. For SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support after December 31st, 2026.  

You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Who do I contact with questions? 

Your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner. Or leave a comment below. 

 

Next Steps

  1. If you use SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI Capabilities — engage your SAP account manager now to plan the AI Units licensing transition before October 1, 2026. Purchase the AI Units contract (SKU 8019164) on the SAP Store. 
  2. If you use SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features or Joule Studio, classic edition genAI features, your access continues through December 31, 2026. After that date, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio once it is generally available in H2 2026. 
  3. If you use the AI chat in SAP Build Code — no action needed. The capability continues in Business Application Studio beyond December 31, 2026 under fair use limits and is enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 
  4. Share this post internally with developers, architects, and project owners who need to plan for these changes.

If you have questions, please leave a comment below or reach out to your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner.

entry.title: SAP BPA RDP: Why We Need Remote Desktop Execution for Scalable Automation
entry.content:
Introduction

A few months ago, I was working on a SAP Build Process Automation (BPA) project that started small — just a handful of users running an Excel-driven automation , worked on my machine, on the test users' machines, and even during the pilot. Then came rollout.

The user base jumped from 20 to a few hundred, with plans to reach 1000+. Suddenly, the install the SAP Desktop Agent on every machine model didn't feel so simple anymore. Some laptops had restricted admin rights, Some users worked outside the company. Every failure ticket had a different root cause agent not running, Excel version mismatch, SSO token expired, machine asleep at scheduled run time.

That's when we made the call: stop running automations on user desktops, and move them to an RDP / VM-based execution model.

A second Use-case:

Requirement: We need an automation that picks up a file and processes it every day at 12:00 AM, 12:00 PM, 3:00 AM, and 3:00 PM.

Simple enough — BPA has a built-in timer trigger for exactly this. I built it, tested it and scheduled it on my local agent.

Then the reality check.

At 3:00 AM, my laptop was off. At 12:00 AM, it was asleep. When I opened it in the morning, BPA happily triggered the job — several hours late. 

Here's the thing nobody tells you when you first start with BPA schedulers:

The timer runs in the cloud, but the automation runs on the agent.
If the agent (your laptop) is off, locked, or disconnected, the trigger just queues up and waits.

So a 3:00 AM job on a developer's laptop is basically a 9:00 AM job whenever the developer walks in.

This is exactly the kind of scenario where an RDP / VM-based agent shines:

  • The VM is always on.
  • The VM is always logged in (under a technical user).
  • The VM is always connected to BPA.
  • The timer fires at 3:00 AM → the VM picks it up at 3:00 AM. Done.

After moving that automation to the VM, the scheduled runs became reliable — which is exactly what you want from a scheduled job.

What is RDP in this context?

In simple terms: instead of the automation running on each end user's laptop, it runs on a centrally managed virtual machine where the SAP Desktop Agent is installed once. Users don't need the agent — they just trigger the process (via a Fiori form, workflow task, or API), and the VM does the heavy lifting.

Workflow Vs Automation

  • Workflow → runs in the cloud, no agent needed.
  • Automation → touches Excel, SAP GUI, PDFs, Outlook → needs an agent → needs a machine.

Once we accepted that automations always need a machine somewhere, the question became: whose machine? Every user's, or one VM we control?

RDP is a solution where the automation runs on a virtual machine (VM) instead of on each user’s personal desktop. In this model, the user does not need to install the agent on their local machine. Instead, the automation is triggered and executed in the VM environment, which is centrally managed.

This is especially useful when:

  • many users need access to the same automation
  • the process must run consistently without depending on a user’s local machine
  • the user machine is not always available or is restricted by security policies
  • you want to reduce installation and maintenance effort

What worked well for us

Here's what genuinely made life easier after the switch:

1. One agent to maintain, not hundreds.
Patching, version upgrades, and Excel/Outlook compatibility issues went from "coordinate with IT for 500 machines" to "log into the VM and fix it once."

2. Runs even when the user is offline.
This was huge. Users would trigger a process at end of day, log off, and go home. The VM continued executing overnight. Previously, the automation would freeze the moment their laptop went to sleep.

3. Cleaner authorization model.
We use a technical user for backend calls on the VM. No more chasing individual user role assignments across S/4HANA.

The challenges nobody warned us about

This is the part I wish someone had written a blog about before we started. So here it is.

Challenge 1: SSO doesn't behave the way you think in a VM

Our first big surprise. The automation was calling a BAPI via the SAP GUI script, and it kept failing with authorization errors — even though the same script worked perfectly on a user's laptop.

The reason: the VM agent runs under a service/technical account, not the actual end user's SSO context. SSO ticket propagation simply doesn't work the way it does on a user's own desktop session.

What we did: switched BAPI-based calls to Basic Authentication with a technical user, and for anything customer-facing, moved to OData actions instead of GUI scripting. Cleaner, faster, and doesn't depend on GUI at all.

Challenge 2: Agent disconnects at the worst possible time

The VM agent occasionally went into a "disconnected" state — usually after Windows updates or network blips. Because we didn't have monitoring on it initially, we only found out when users complained that their tasks were stuck.

solution:

  • Added an alert on the BPA agent status.

Challenge 3: File and folder access

The automation reads Excel files uploaded by users. On a desktop setup, this was easy — the file was already local. On the VM, we had to build an upload path: user uploads via a form → file lands in a shared folder (or SAP Document Management) → VM picks it up.

Small architectural change, but it caught us mid-project.

Challenge 4: Session locking on the VM

If someone RDP into the VM interactively and locked the screen, some automations (especially GUI-based ones) would fail because the desktop session was locked. We ended up disabling interactive login for the technical user during business hours.

When to use a Local Desktop Agent vs. an RDP / VM Agent

Go with a Local Desktop Agent when:
  • The automation is used by a single user or a very small group (say, < 10 users).
  • The user needs to watch it run or interact with it (attended automation).
  • The trigger is manual — the user clicks a button, opens a form, or launches it from the BPA store.
  • The automation genuinely needs the user's own SSO context (e.g., personal Outlook, personal drives).
  • It's a quick PoC or pilot where you don't want VM infrastructure yet.
Go with RDP / VM-based execution when:
  • The automation is scheduled (timer-based): daily, hourly, midnight runs, etc.
  • Many users need to trigger the same automation.
  • The process must run unattended — no one is watching, no one is logged in.
  • You need reliable, predictable runtime independent of any user's laptop.
  • You want centralized monitoring, logging, and error handling.
  • You're connecting to backend systems with a technical user / Basic Auth.
  • You're worried about rollout, patching, or supporting the agent across many machines.

Configuration checklist we now use

Before going live with any VM-based BPA automation, we run through this list. Sharing it here so you don't have to build one from scratch:

  •  VM agent is registered in BPA and shows as connected/healthy
  • Excel, Outlook, SAP GUI, and PDF viewer are installed and licensed on the VM
  • Shared folders / network drives / DMS paths are accessible from the VM
  • Technical user has required S/4HANA / backend role assignments
  • Basic Authentication configured for BAPI-based destinations (not SSO)
  • Session lock policy on the VM is handled (don't let RDP sessions lock during runs)
  • Windows Update / patch window is scheduled outside automation run times
  • Monitoring/alerting on agent status is in place
  • End-to-end test with a real trigger, real file, real user — not just a dev sandbox
Not everything in BPA needs an agent. Design your process so that the workflow part (approvals, decisions, notifications) stays in the cloud, and only the desktop-dependent automation part touches the VM.

Conclusion

Moving to RDP / VM-based execution it was one of the highest-impact changes in the project. It turned a fragile, hard-to-support automation into something we now confidently run for hundreds of users — with a clear path to scaling further.

If you're at the point where you're installing the SAP Desktop Agent on your fifth, tenth, or hundredth user machine — pause. Consider whether a VM-based setup would save you months of support pain later.

Key takeaways in one line each:

  • Workflow can run agentless. Automation almost always needs an agent — the question is where.
  • One VM > many user desktops, once you cross a small user threshold.
  • Use Basic Auth with a technical user for BAPI calls in VM context. SSO won't behave as expected.
  • Prefer OData actions over GUI scripting wherever possible.

This approach makes the process more reliable, scalable, and easier to manage in enterprise environments.

entry.title: From Inbox to Folder: Fetching Gmail Attachments with SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Connecting SAP Build Process Automation to Google Workspace, so invoice PDFs arriving in a Gmail inbox land in a local folder, ready for extraction and approval.

Introduction

This is the fourth post in the series. In the first post, we built the core invoice approval workflow in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA). In the second, we connected to a trial Document AI instance, and in the third, we wired extraction straight into the approval process. Throughout, the invoice PDFs were simply sitting in a folder, put there by hand.

In practice, invoices arrive by email. So in this post we remove that last manual step: a task automation connects to Google Workspace, searches a Gmail inbox for invoice emails, and saves the PDF attachments into a folder on the machine running the Desktop Agent. That folder is then what the extraction and approval flow reads from.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Creating an OAuth 2.0 Client ID in Google Cloud Console
  • Creating the External Authentication in BPA Control Tower
  • Registering the authentication on the Desktop Agent and giving consent
  • Building a task automation that searches Gmail and downloads attachments
  • Testing it with a real email

Choosing How to Connect to Google Workspace

BPA offers a few ways to authorize against Google Workspace. Authorize Google (OAuth Client ID) and Authorize Google (Service Account) are activities placed inside the automation, and both work on Desktop Agent 2 and 3. Select Google Authentication works differently: the OAuth client is configured once in Control Tower, registered once on the Desktop Agent, and the automation simply selects it by name.

We'll use Select Google Authentication, which requires Desktop Agent 3 (SAP documents version 3.16 or higher for Google external authorization). No credentials live inside the automation itself, which keeps the project clean.

Step 1: Set Up the OAuth Client in Google Cloud Console

Everything starts on the Google side. Open the Google Cloud Console and select the project you want to work in. Under APIs & Services, the Credentials page shows the OAuth consent screen, the Create credentials button, and any OAuth 2.0 Client IDs already created.

 

APIs & Services > Credentials in the selected Google Cloud project.

  1. Enable the APIs. Under Enabled APIs & services, enable the Google Workspace APIs you plan to use. I enabled the Gmail API, Google Calendar API and Google Drive API. Only Gmail is used in this post, but the others save a trip back later.
  2. Configure the OAuth consent screen. On the Branding page of Google Auth Platform, give the app a name (mine is SAP-BPA-Test, which is what users see when they sign in) and a user support email.

 

Branding --- app name and user support email.

  1. Scroll down to the app domain fields and the developer contact email. The domain fields (home page, privacy policy, terms of service) can stay empty for a testing setup.

 

Branding, continued --- app domain, authorized domains and developer contact information.

  1. Set the Audience. I chose the External user type and left the publishing status as Testing. While in Testing, only listed test users can authorize the app, so add your own Gmail address under Test users.

 

Audience --- External user type, Testing status, and the test user list.

  1. Add scopes under Data Access. Scopes define what the app is allowed to do with the account. I added userinfo.email, cloud-platform, calendar, drive and the Gmail scope (https://mail.google.com/). Google groups Drive and Gmail under restricted scopes, which is why they get a stricter consent flow.

 

Data Access --- the non-sensitive, sensitive and restricted scopes added to the app.

  1. Create the client. Under Clients, create a new OAuth client with the application type Desktop app. I named mine Desktop Agent BPA. Google generates a Client ID and a Client secret, and you can also download them as a clientid.json file. Control Tower needs exactly these two values.

 

The Desktop client --- Client ID and client secret (sensitive parts hidden).

Treat the client secret like a password, and keep it out of screenshots and source control.

Step 2: Create the External Authentication in Control Tower

Now we move to SAP Build. From the Lobby, open Control Tower > External Authentication. This is where BPA stores the OAuth client details for the tenant. The screenshot below already shows one entry, Google Workspace Test, along with the Create New Authentication button.

 

Control Tower > External Authentication.

  1. Choose Google as the type of external portal, then enter a unique Name (this is the name you'll select in the automation later) and an optional Description.
  2. Paste the Client ID and Client Secret from the Google client (the clientid.json values).
  3. Select the scopes. User Email is pre-selected and mandatory. The list also offers Calendar, Cloud Platform, Drive and Gmail. I selected only Gmail for now, so the consent screen stays short and the permissions stay minimal. You can always create another authentication later with more scopes.

 

The Create Authentication dialog for Google.

Step 3: Register It on the Desktop Agent

The authentication exists on the tenant, but it isn't usable until the Desktop Agent on your machine registers it.

  1. In the Desktop Agent, click the Settings gear and choose External Authentication.

 

Desktop Agent --- Settings > External Authentication.

  1. The tenant's authentications are listed with their type and status. Open the one you created.

 

The external authentication listed in the Desktop Agent.

  1. Enter the email address of the Google account to use. You can mark the authentication as Default, so automations fall back to it when no name is given. Once it shows Registered, it can also be unregistered from this same screen.

 

The registered authentication, with the email address hidden.

Registering opens Google's sign-in flow in the browser. The first screen confirms which account is signing in to the app we named on the Branding page.

 

Sign in with Google --- confirming the account for SAP-BPA-Test.

The second screen lists what the app wants to access, which here is the Gmail permission we selected in Control Tower. Because the app is in Testing and unverified, Google's wording is a bit more cautious. Review it and click Continue.

 

The consent screen requesting Gmail access.

That's the whole one-time setup. Any automation running on this Desktop Agent can now use the registered Google account.

Step 4: Build the Task Automation

With authorization in place, we can build the automation itself. I added a task automation, InvoiceApprovalAutomation, to the same project that holds the invoice approval process. For this post the flow is deliberately small: authenticate, search the inbox, clean the target folder, download the attachments, and log the result.

The Test Email

To test, I sent myself an email with a recognizable subject, Gmail-BPA, and three invoice PDFs attached. The automation searches for exactly that subject, so it only picks up emails meant for it.

 

The test email in the Gmail inbox --- three PDF attachments, ready to be read by the Desktop Agent.

Building the Flow

  1. Select Google Authentication. The first activity takes the name of the external authentication as its only input. Pick the one you registered (in my case, Google Workspace Test). If it's left empty, the default registered authentication is used. The activity can throw a GoogleAuthError.

 

Select Google Authentication --- the name of the registered external authentication.

  1. Try / Catch. Everything that talks to Gmail sits inside a Try block that catches GmailError, so a failure (an expired token, for example) can be handled and logged rather than crashing the automation halfway.

 

The Try block, catching GmailError.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail). The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), which looks in the inbox for messages with our keyword in the subject. The usual Gmail search operators work here, so you can narrow it further (for example with is:unread or has:attachment). includeSpamTrash is set to false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) --- query on the inbox label and subject.

  1. Email Found? A Condition step checks messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If at least one email matches, the flow continues. Otherwise, the default branch just logs that nothing was found, which is a normal outcome for a scheduled run on an empty inbox.

 

The Email Found? condition.

  1. Delete All Files. Before downloading, this activity empties the target folder (GmailFileFromAgent in my case), so attachments from earlier runs aren't picked up by extraction a second time.

 

Delete All Files --- clearing the target folder before each run.

  1. Read Email (Gmail). This downloads the message. messageId is set to messageIdentifiers[0].messageId (the first match), location is fileSystem so the attachments are written to disk (the alternative is Google Drive), and pathOrDriveId is the folder we just cleaned. markAsRead is optional, and the output messageDetail holds the email details.

 

Read Email (Gmail) --- saving the attachments to the file system.

Running It

I ran the automation from the designer in unattended mode. The test console shows each step completing in order (Select Google Authentication, Search Emails, Delete All Files, Read Email, Log Message, End), and the target folder now holds the three PDF attachments from the test email.

 

The test run, with the three invoice PDFs saved into the target folder.

The greyed-out steps lower in the flow (Get File Collection, the For Each loop, DocAI - Extract with Schema and InvoiceApprovalProcess) are disabled for this run. They're the extraction and approval part from the earlier posts, which is where this folder gets used next.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • One email per run. Because the message ID comes from index 0, this flow handles the first matching email. If several invoice emails can arrive between runs, loop over messageIdentifiers and use markAsRead so each is handled once.
  • Testing-mode token expiry. For an External app in Testing status, Google limits how long a refresh token stays valid (documented as seven days). If the automation asks for authorization again after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again. Publishing the app avoids this, but brings Google's verification process into play, especially for the Gmail scope.
  • Test users only. If Google blocks the sign-in, check that your account is on the Test users list.
  • Scopes. If Gmail calls fail with permission errors, check that the Gmail scope was selected in the External Authentication, then unregister and register again so the new scope is granted.

Wrapping Up

Connecting BPA to Gmail takes a few moving parts: a Google OAuth client, an External Authentication in Control Tower, a registration on the Desktop Agent, and one activity in the automation. Once that's done, it's a reusable foundation. The same setup can later send emails (for example approval replies), change labels on processed mails, or work with Drive and Calendar if you add those scopes.

With invoice PDFs now landing in a folder straight from an inbox, the next step is to switch the extraction and approval steps back on, so that an email arriving in Gmail ends up as an approval task in My Inbox, and the decision goes back out by email, all from within the task automation.

entry.title: Every Gmail Activity in SAP Build Process Automation: Search, Read, Label, Send, Reply and Delete
entry.content:
A hands-on walkthrough of the Gmail activities in the Google Workspace SDK, built into a single task automation and tested against real emails.

Introduction

This is the fifth post in the series. In the previous post, we set up the Google OAuth client, created the External Authentication in Control Tower, registered it on the Desktop Agent, and built a small automation that searches Gmail and saves attachments to a local folder. That post ended with one search, one read, and a folder of PDFs.

Gmail offers a lot more than that. In this post we go through every Gmail activity BPA provides, one at a time, inside a single task automation. Along the way we make sure an email is never read twice, send a fresh email with attachments, reply to a thread, and finally delete an email.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Searching Gmail and reading an email, with its attachments saved to a local folder
  • Moving a processed email from Inbox to a "read" label, so it's never fetched again
  • Sending an email with attachments
  • Replying and replying to all on an existing thread
  • Deleting an email (and why that one deserves extra care)
  • Cleaning up with Disconnect (Google)

The Gmail Activities at a Glance

With the Google Workspace SDK added to the project, searching for "Gmail" in the automation's Tools panel lists seven activities: Send Email, Search Emails, Read Email, Modify Email Labels, Send Reply, Reply All and Delete Email. It also lists the supporting data types, such as Gmail Attachments, Gmail Message Detail, Gmail Message Identifier, Gmail Parameters and Gmail Reply Parameters. Every activity we use in this post is highlighted below in red.

 

The finished automation with each Gmail activity highlighted, next to the Gmail activities in the Tools panel.

The flow reads top to bottom, and each group of steps maps to one part of this post:

  • Steps 3 to 6: search the inbox, check that something was found, empty the target folder, and read the email with its attachments.
  • Step 7: modify the labels on the email we just read.
  • Step 8: send a new email with attachments.
  • Steps 10 to 12: search for a thread, then reply to all and reply to it.
  • Steps 13 and 14: search for a temporary email and delete it.
  • Step 15: disconnect from Google.

Everything from step 1 (Select Google Authentication) sits inside the same Try / Catch pattern from the previous post, catching GmailError.

Before You Start

  • The External Authentication from the previous post needs the Gmail scope. That scope covers reading, sending and permanently deleting email, so nothing extra is needed for this post. If you ever add a scope, update the External Authentication in Control Tower and register it on the Desktop Agent again.
  • Create a Gmail label named BPA-Read manually in Gmail. The automation applies this label but does not create it.
  • Prepare three test emails with distinct subjects, so each part of the flow only touches its own email: Gmail-BPA (with three PDF attachments) for read and label, BPA-Gmail (a thread with a few participants) for the reply steps, and BPA-Delete for the delete step.
  • Use a test mailbox. The delete step is permanent.

Part 1: Search and Read an Email

This part repeats the idea from the previous post, so I'll keep it brief. The test email sits in the Inbox, with the subject Gmail-BPA and three invoice PDFs attached.

 

The test email in the Inbox, with three PDF attachments.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail). I renamed this step "Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments" so it's easy to tell apart from the other searches later in the flow. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), so only emails still in the Inbox with that subject are returned. includeSpamTrash is false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments.

  1. Email Found? A Condition step checks Step3.messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If nothing matches, the default branch just logs a message.

 

The Email Found? condition.

  1. Delete All Files. Before downloading, this empties the local target folder, so files from an earlier run are never picked up again.

 

Delete All Files on the target folder.

  1. Read Email (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, location is fileSystem, and pathOrDriveId is the same target folder. The three PDFs are saved there, and the output messageDetail holds the email details.

 

Read Email (Gmail) saving the three attachments into the target folder.

Part 2: Modify Email Labels

Here is a problem with the flow so far: the email stays in the Inbox after we read it, so the next run would find and read it again. We solve that with Modify Email Labels (Gmail), which moves the email out of the Inbox and into our BPA-Read label. Because the search query includes Label: Inbox, an email that has been moved never matches again.

  1. Modify Email Labels (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, the same email we just read. labelsToAdd is a list holding BPA-Read, and labelsToRemove is a list holding Inbox. Both lists are entered as custom data, one string per label.

 

Modify Email Labels (Gmail) adding BPA-Read and removing Inbox.

Back in Gmail, the same email now carries the BPA-Read label instead of Inbox.

 

The processed email, now labelled BPA-Read.

This is the label approach I chose over the markAsRead option on Read Email. The email keeps its read or unread state, and the label gives you a visible record of what the automation has handled, which you can also search on in Gmail.

Part 3: Send Email

Next we send a new email using Send Email (Gmail). All its inputs live in one custom data object called gmailParameters.

  1. Fill in the recipient fields: to, plus optional cc and bcc (semicolon separated). I sent it to my own address for the test.
  2. Set the subject ([BPA Auto] Invoice Attachments | Send Mail) and the body. isHtmlBody is false here, so the body is plain text. Set it to true if you want to send HTML.

 

Send Email (Gmail) --- recipients, subject, body and the start of the attachments list.

  1. Add attachments. Each attachment is its own entry with attachFrom (fileSystem here) and a filePath. I attached the same three PDFs we downloaded in Part 1, purely for convenience. Any file path works, so you can attach whatever your scenario needs.

 

One attachment entry per file, each with attachFrom and filePath.

The email arrives with all three PDFs attached.

 

The email sent by the automation, with its three attachments.

Part 4: Reply and Reply All

To reply to an existing conversation, the automation needs to know which thread to reply into. For this I set up a separate test thread with a few participants, subject BPA-Gmail, and added a dedicated search step for it.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Gmail"), and the output is again messageIdentifiers, this time from step 10.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply.

  1. Reply All (Gmail). The input is replyParamters (the spelling as it appears in the activity). threadId is messageIdentifiers[0].threadId from step 10, which is what places the reply inside the existing conversation. messageId, to, cc and bcc are left empty, and the body is the text to send. includeOriginalAttachments is false, and attachments can be added the same way as in Send Email.

 

Reply All (Gmail), with threadId taken from the search step.

  1. Send Reply (Gmail). It has the same parameters as Reply All. The difference is in who receives the message: Reply All goes to everyone on the thread, while Send Reply goes back to a single recipient.

 

Send Reply (Gmail), with the same parameter structure.

In Gmail, both messages show up inside the original thread. In my test, the Reply All message went to all four other participants, and the Reply went to one.

 

The test thread, with the Reply All and Reply messages sent by the automation at the bottom.

Part 5: Delete Email

The last activity is Delete Email (Gmail). As with replying, we first find the email, this time using a dedicated search step with the subject BPA-Delete.

  1. Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Delete"), and the output messageIdentifiers comes from step 13.

 

Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete.

  1. Delete Email (Gmail). The only required input is messageId, here messageIdentifiers[0].messageId from step 13.

 

Delete Email (Gmail) with the messageId from the search step.

This is the temporary email the automation removes:

 

The temporary email, before the automation runs.

This deletion is permanent. When you delete an email in the Gmail interface, it moves to Trash and is removed later, either after Gmail's retention period or when you empty the Trash yourself. The Delete Email activity does not do that. In my test the email was gone immediately and did not appear in Trash, which matches how Google describes the underlying delete call in the Gmail API: immediate and permanent, with no way to undo it. Treat this activity like a delete statement without a rollback.

Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google)

The last step of the flow, step 15, is Disconnect (Google), which closes the connection to Google once the work is done. It sits after the Try / Catch block, so it runs on both the success and error paths.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • Be careful with delete. Use a precise query (here, a keyword unique to the temporary email), run it against a test mailbox first, and consider whether a label like BPA-Delete or a separate review step is safer for production scenarios.
  • Guard the later steps. In this flow, steps 10 to 14 sit outside the Email Found? condition, and they read messageIdentifiers[0]. If a search returns no results, that step has nothing to read. Wrapping each search-then-act pair in its own condition, like we did for step 4, avoids that.
  • First match only. Using index 0 means each run handles one email per search. For several emails, loop over messageIdentifiers.
  • Labels must exist. Modify Email Labels uses the label names you enter, so create BPA-Read in Gmail first and keep the spelling identical.
  • Gmail search syntax. The query field accepts the same operators as the Gmail search bar, so you can narrow results further (for example, by sender or date).
  • Testing-mode token expiry. As noted in the previous post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization suddenly fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again.

Wrapping Up

With these seven activities, a BPA automation can do nearly everything you'd do by hand in a Gmail inbox: find an email, read it and save its attachments, mark it as processed, send a new message, reply into a thread, and, when needed, delete one for good. They all run on the single setup from the previous post.

If you want to take this further into a complete invoice flow, you can combine the pieces from this series yourself. Each post covers one layer: the first builds the invoice approval process, the second sets up Document AI extraction on a trial instance, the third wires extraction into the approval process, and the fourth connects BPA to Google Workspace and fetches the attachments. This post adds the remaining Gmail activities on top of that setup. The fetched PDFs from the Gmail steps can serve as the source folder for the extraction automation in the second and third posts.

Each part is covered and tested on its own, and the connection points (a folder of PDFs, then extraction, then a call to the approval process) are the same ones those posts already use. If you would like the decision to go back to the sender as a reply in the original email thread, the Send Reply and Reply All activities are the ones to look at. The approval emails in the earlier posts are sent from the process itself, so that part would need some extra wiring.

entry.title: An End-to-End Travel Approval App with SAP CAP, HANA Cloud, and SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Goal

The goal is to build a working Travel Approval application, not just a collection of disconnected demos. A user creates a travel request in a Fiori Elements application. The CAP service stores the request in SAP HANA Cloud and automatically starts an SAP Build Process Automation workflow.

The approver reviews the task in My Inbox and selects Approve or Reject, updating the corresponding Travel record in HANA Cloud.

Create Travel in Fiori
       ↓
CAP saves the active record in HANA Cloud
       ↓
CAP starts the BPA workflow automatically
       ↓
Approval task appears in SAP Build Lobby->My Inbox
       ↓
Approve → overall_status = A
Reject → overall_status = R
       ↓
Validate in Fiori, SAP Build->Monitoring, and HANA Database Explorer

Prerequisites

BTP Service / instance required
SAP Business Application Studio
SAP HANA Cloud
SAP Build Process Automation

The End-to-End Flow

  1. Create Travel entity in CDS.
  2. Expose the entity as a draft-enabled OData V4 service.
  3. Generate the Fiori Elements application.
  4. Bind the CAP project to the HANA HDI container.
  5. Build the MTA archive and deploy it to Cloud Foundry.
  6. Download the CAP metadata as an EDMX specification.
  7. Create SAP Build Actions from the EDMX and test the OData operations.
  8. Create the Travel Context, API trigger, Approval Form, and approval branches in BPA.
  9. Create a BPA service key and an API key with trigger execution permission.
  10. Add the CAP SAVE handler that starts the workflow automatically.
  11. Test from Fiori, process the task in My Inbox, monitor the instance in Build Lobby, and validate the final status in HANA.

1. Model the CDS Entity for the CAP OData V4 Service

The CDS entity is the source of truth for the Travel data. The technical UUID and the business Travel ID form the key used by the draft-enabled service and by the generated SAP Build Actions.

1.1.    Expose the Travel entity as a service

Create file srv/service.cds.

Why draft support matters: Fiori Elements creates and edits a draft first. The active Travel record is produced when the user activates or saves the draft. The CAP SAVE event is therefore the reliable point for starting the workflow.

2. Create the Fiori Elements App

Generate a List Report/Object Page application for CAPWFService.Travel. The list lets users create requests and review the current status. The Object Page captures the full Travel details.

 

Figure 1. Fiori List Report with Travel IDs in ascending order.

3. Connect to Cloud Foundry

3.1.    Cloud Foundry provides the runtime for the deployed CAP service. Log in from the BAS terminal and select the correct organization and dev space.

cf login
cf target

3.2.    Before testing SAP Build Actions, always confirm that the deployed CAP application is running:

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

3.3.    Expected status:

requested state: started
instances: 1/1
state: running

Important: When CAPWF-srv was stopped, every SAP Build Action returned 404 Requested route does not exist. Starting the application restored the Actions immediately.

4. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container

An HDI container is an application-scoped database container. It gives the CAP application its own isolated schema inside the HANA Cloud database.

cds bind --to CAPWF-db
cds env get requires.db --profile hybrid

The hybrid profile must show the CAPWF-db instance. Start the local service against HANA:

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

Look for connect to db > hana and the expected HANA schema in the terminal output.

Lesson learned: The lowercase capwf-db and uppercase CAPWF-db were two separate service instances. Local Fiori and deployed BPA initially showed different record counts because they were connected to different HDI containers.

5. Generate the MTAR File

The Multi-Target Application archive packages the service, database deployer, security resources, destinations, and HTML5 content into one deployable unit.

mbt build

The archive is generated under: mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

6. Deploy to HANA Cloud and Cloud Foundry

cf deploy mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

The deployment runs the database deployer, binds CAPWF-srv to CAPWF-db and CAPWF-auth, and starts the application route.

cf app CAPWF-srv
cf routes
cf logs CAPWF-srv --recent

Free-tier note: Stopping applications frees runtime memory, but it also makes the CAP route unavailable. Start CAPWF-srv again before testing browser URLs or SAP Build Actions.

7. Connect to the HANA DB Explorer and Add the HDI Container

7.1.    Open SAP HANA Database Explorer.

7.2.    Choose Add Database or Add HDI Container.

7.3.    Select the CAPWF-db HDI container.

7.4.    Expand Catalog and Tables.

7.5.    Open the Travel table data and compare the record count with the Fiori app.

7.6.    After approval or rejection, refresh the table and verify overall_status.

Figure 2. CAPWF-db added to SAP HANA Database Explorer.

8. Download the Metadata File as EDMX

The metadata document describes the OData V4 service, entity fields, keys, draft properties, and custom actions. SAP Build uses this specification to generate reusable Actions.

/service/CAPWFService/$metadata

Open the metadata->right-click->Save as .edmx file

Open the local BAS port 4004 metadata URL, save the XML as CAPWFService.edmx, and verify that it contains:

  • EntitySet Name="Travel"
  • The Travel entity fields and keys
  • Draft operations
  • Action Name="submitForApproval" IsBound="true"

9. Create SAP Build Actions

9.1. Open SAP Build Lobby -> Actions -> Create.

9.2. Choose Upload API Specification.

9.3. Upload CAPWFService.edmx.

9.4. Create the Action project CAPWFService3.

9.5. Select the required Travel operations. The POC selected all 13 generated operations.

10.   Open Settings and configure the destination and URL prefix.

SettingValue
DestinationCAPWF-srv
URL Prefix/service/CAPWFService
CSRFDisabled for this POC
Destination authenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials

11.   Test the Actions before publishing

11.1.   Get entities from Travel should return 200 OK and all records. - see the image below

11.2.   Get entity from Travel by key should return the selected record using ID, travel_id, and  IsActiveEntity=true.

11.3.   Update entity in Travel should be validated independently before adding it to the process.

11.4.   Release and Publish only after direct tests succeed.

cf logs CAPWF-srv cf app CAPWF-srv cf start CAPWF-srv -->You can see the Instances are up and Running 1/14.       The root cause may simply be a stopped application.

Troubleshooting shortcut: If all Actions suddenly return 404 and no request reaches, run the below commands in new Terminal.

 

Figure 2. CAPWFService3 Action test returning 200 OK.

12. Steps in SAP Build Process Automation

12.1.Create the project and artifacts

12.2.Create the project RAP110_Travel_Workflow.

12.3.Create the process of Travel Approval Processing.

12.4.Create the Travel Context datatype.

12.5.Create a Travel Approval Trigger as an API trigger.

12.6.Create the Approval Form and map the Travel fields.

12.7.Add Approve and Reject outcomes.

12.8.Add Update entity in Travel from the published CAPWFService3 dependency.

12.9.Map the keys and set overall_status to A in Approve and R in Reject.

13. Travel Context fields

FieldData Type
TravelUUIDString
TravelIDNumber
IsActiveEntityBoolean
agency_idNumber
customer_idNumber
begin_dateDate
end_dateDate
booking_feeNumber
total_priceNumber
currency_codeString
descriptionString
overall_statusString

14. Approval Form recipient

When a human starts the workflow manually, Started By is the signed-in user. When CAP starts the process using client credentials, Started By is a technical client. For the POC, the Approval Form recipient was set to the intended email address, so the work item appeared in My Inbox. A production design should pass an ApproverEmail value or determine the approver through business rules.

15. Add and Delete Dependencies

15.1.A process can use only released and published Action projects through Dependencies.

15.2.Open the editable BPA project and switch to Dependencies.

15.3.Add the published CAPWFService3 Action project.

15.4.If an old Action dependency is removed, delete any orphaned process nodes that show blank Inputs.

15.5.Re-add the Actions from CAPWFService3 and remap their inputs.

15.6.To remove a dependency, select it, choose Settings, and select Delete.

15.7.If an Action project cannot be deleted, remove consuming dependencies and delete its released versions first.

16. Create an API Key in SAP Build

The CAP application starts the process as a technical client. It therefore needs both OAuth client credentials and an SAP Build API key that is authorized to execute the trigger.

16.1.Open SAP Build -> Control Tower -> API Keys, or Public Environment -> API Keys.

16.2.Choose Add API Key.

16.3.Enter a meaningful name, such as CAPWF_Auto_Start.

16.4.Select the Public environment.

16.5.Enable trigger_execute. This is the minimum scope needed to execute the API trigger.

16.6.Create the key and copy it immediately. The value is displayed only once.

17. Build Process Automation - Manual Workflow Test Using the Payload

Before automating the trigger from CAP, manually prove the deployed process and payload schema.

17.1.Open Control Tower -> Environments -> Public -> Triggers.

17.2.Open Travel Approval Trigger.

17.3.Choose Start New Instance.

17.4.Paste only the process context expected by the dialog, with travelContext as the root object.

17.5.Start the instance and confirm it appears in Monitoring.

17.6.Open My Inbox and process the task.

17.7.Confirm the instance completes and the Travel status is updated.

{
"travelContext": {
   "TravelUUID": "<UUID>",
   "TravelID": 15,
   "IsActiveEntity": true,
   "agency_id": 70015,
   "customer_id": 70015,
   "begin_date": "2026-10-02",
   "end_date": "2026-10-16",
   "booking_fee": 150,
   "total_price": 150,
   "currency_code": "INR",
   "description": "Travel request",
   "overall_status": "W"
}
}

18. List of Terminal Commands to Get BPA Keys

cf create-service-key BPA cap-bpa-key
cf service-key BPA cap-bpa-key

From the BPA service key, record these values securely: clientid, clientsecret, and URL. The token endpoint is the URL value plus /oauth/token.

Do not mix credentials: CAPWF-auth credentials protect the CAP application. BPA service-key credentials authenticate the call to SAP Build Process Automation. Using CAPWF-auth credentials caused 401 invalid_client / Bad credentials.

19. Start the Workflow Automatically from CAP

The Fiori application activates a draft when the user saves a new Travel. CAP handles that lifecycle through the SAVE event. The handler builds the exact trigger payload, obtains an OAuth token, sends the BPA API key, and creates the workflow instance.

// create a file in srv/service.js

this.after('SAVE', 'Travel', async (data, req) => {
   const travel = req.data;

   const workflowPayload = {
       definitionId:
         'us10.e66895ddtrial.rap110travelworkflow.travelApprovalProcessing',
       context: {
           travelContext: {
               TravelUUID: travel.ID,
               TravelID: travel.travel_id,
               IsActiveEntity: true,
               agency_id: travel.agency_id,
               customer_id: travel.customer_id,
               begin_date: travel.begin_date,
               end_date: travel.end_date,
               booking_fee: Number(travel.booking_fee),
               total_price: Number(travel.total_price),
               currency_code: travel.currency_code,
               description: travel.description,
               overall_status: travel.overall_status
           }
       }
   };

   // 1. Get an OAuth token with BPA client credentials.
   // 2. POST workflowPayload to BPA_WORKFLOW_URL.
   // 3. Send Authorization: Bearer <token> and api-key headers.
});

20. Verify in BAS with Three Terminals

20.1.   Terminal 1 - Run local CAP with BPA credentials

export BPA_CLIENT_ID='<BPA service-key clientid>'
export BPA_CLIENT_SECRET='<BPA service-key clientsecret>'
export BPA_TOKEN_URL='<BPA service-key url>/oauth/token'
export BPA_API_KEY='<SAP Build Public environment API key>'
export BPA_WORKFLOW_URL='https://spa-api-gateway-bpi-us-prod.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com/workflow/rest/v1/workflow-instances'

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

20.2.   Terminal 2 - Confirm the deployed CAP app is running

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

20.3.   Terminal 3 - Watch deployed CAP requests

cf logs CAPWF-srv

A successful automatic start prints:

BPA workflow started for Travel 5
Workflow instance ID: <generated instance ID>

Session behavior: The export commands apply only to the current terminal session.

After BAS signs out or a new terminal is opened, export the variables again before cds watch.

21. Test Directly from the Fiori Application

21.1.Confirm Terminal 1 has BPA environment variables, and cds watch is running.

21.2.Confirm CAPWF-srv is 1/1 running if the workflow will call CAP through SAP Build Actions.

21.3.Open the Fiori Preview.

21.4.Create a new Travel record with overall_status W.

21.5.Save the record.

21.6.Watch Terminal 1 for the workflow instance ID.

21.7.Open SAP Build My Inbox and process the Travel task.

21.8.Refresh the Fiori List Report and confirm A or R.

22. My Inbox - Approve or Reject

The approver opens the Travel task, reviews the Travel fields, and chooses Approve or Reject. The process follows the corresponding branch and calls the CAP update Action. The completed workflow should disappear from My Inbox and appear as Completed in Monitoring.

If My Inbox is empty: Open the instance Logs. If the recipient is a technical client instead of the intended user, revise the Approval Form recipient mapping and deploy a new version.

23. Monitor Workflow Instances

23.1.Open SAP Build -> Monitoring -> Processes and Workflows.

23.2.Open Travel Approval Processing.

23.3.Filter by Running, Error, or Completed.

23.4.Open an instance and inspect Logs to see each executed step.

23.5.Open Context to confirm startEvent.travelContext values.

23.6.Use the instance ID printed by CAP to correlate the application request with the workflow instance.

Figure 4. Completed Travel Approval Processing instance.

24. Validate in the HDI Container

24.1.Open SAP HANA Database Explorer and refresh CAPWF-db.

24.2.Open the Travel table data.

24.3.Locate the Travel ID used in the test.

24.4.Confirm W before approval.

24.5.Confirm A after approval or R after rejection.

24.6.Compare the result with the Fiori List Report.

What Broke, Why It Broke, and the Fix

pkill -f cds​then start one runtime.

SymptomRoot causeFix
Fiori showed more records than BPA/HANADifferent HDI containers were usedBind local hybrid runtime to CAPWF-db.
Port 4004 already in useAn old cds process was still running
