entry.title: Decision Authority in SAP AI Agents: A Procurement Perspective
entry.content:
Introduction

As enterprise AI moves toward autonomous agents, we tend to measure progress through technical capabilities: how many tasks an agent can complete, how many systems it can connect to, and how much human intervention it can eliminate from existing business processes.

But I believe there is a more fundamental question above all: Who actually holds the authority to make a business decision, humans or AI?

Consider an AI agent supporting procurement in an SAP environment. Let's assume it can retrieve supplier information, compare prices, evaluate delivery schedules, initiate purchase orders, and perhaps even coordinate parts of the supply chain.

None of these capabilities necessarily means it has the authority to select a supplier.

In my research on Decision Authority and Agentic Commerce, I distinguish between executing a task, exercising judgment, and being authorized to determine an outcome. The differences go far beyond technical capabilities.

The transition from execution to decision-making is not simply a technical upgrade. It potentially changes an entire set of relationships involving organizational authority, legal accountability, ethical obligations, and responsibility for consequences.

SAP's enterprise ecosystem provides a useful setting to examine this distinction. Joule Studio supports the development of AI agents. SAP Build Process Automation supports structured business processes, while SAP S/4HANA provides a foundation for enterprise operations.

The question is not simply whether these technologies can support increasingly autonomous workflows. It is how enterprises should define the boundaries of that autonomy.

1. A Procurement Scenario

Imagine a manufacturer running its purchasing operations on SAP S/4HANA.

It needs to replenish an industrial component. Three suppliers are available:

Supplier A: $92 per unit, 21-day delivery, low risk.
Supplier B: $85 per unit, 35-day delivery, medium risk.
Supplier C: $101 per unit, 7-day delivery, low risk.

A procurement agent could retrieve these quotations, compare the alternatives, and recommend Supplier B because it offers the lowest price.

But suppose the manufacturer's production schedule shows that waiting 35 days would create a costly delay.

Supplier C might now be the better choice.

This is where judgment becomes important. The agent must interpret the purchasing requirement within a broader business context rather than simply rank quotations.

Let's move to the next step. Should the agent be allowed to select Supplier C and proceed with the purchasing process?

My answer is that it depends on the authority the enterprise has granted to the agent.

Some organizations may require human approval for every supplier selection. Others may authorize AI to make certain decisions independently, while assigning responsibility for the process, or particular parts of it, to designated people.

An agent may be allowed to make subordinate decisions, handle lower-risk transactions, or complete purchases within predefined financial and operational limits.

All these arrangements are possible, even when the underlying AI capabilities are similar.

The distinction is not primarily about whether the model can identify a reasonable choice. It involves a much broader relationship between the organization, the technology, and the people responsible for its decisions.

It is about whether the organization permits the model to turn its judgment into a binding business action.

I therefore see three separate dimensions:

Execution: What actions can the agent perform?

Judgment: How does it evaluate competing alternatives?

Decision Authority: Which outcomes is it authorized to determine?

An enterprise agent can be highly capable in the first two dimensions while remaining restricted in the third.

2. SAP Architecture and Decision Authority

Technical Scope and Environment

This article presents a conceptual architecture using SAP Joule Studio, SAP Build Process Automation, and SAP S/4HANA. References to purchase order approval mechanisms are based on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition documentation, including Flexible Workflow for Purchase Orders, documentation version 2608.

The proposed architecture has not been implemented or tested in a live SAP environment. Feature availability, integration requirements, and authorization behavior may vary by product edition, release, and system configuration.

SAP Joule Studio

Joule Studio enables organizations to build and use AI agents and connect them for enterprise applications.

In our procurement scenario, a customized agent could be designed to review purchasing needs, retrieve the information it requires, and generate different options or recommendations.

The agent might examine inventory levels, historical consumption, delivery requirements, and purchasing objectives.

However, its ability to evaluate information and make recommendations should remain separate from allowing it to execute transactions directly without permission.

The authorization boundary should be enforced by enterprise controls, rather than left to the model's own judgment.

SAP S/4HANA

SAP S/4HANA provides important operational context for enterprise decisions.

For example, a procurement recommendation becomes more useful when it considers the company's actual situation, including inventory, purchasing requirements, financial information, and other relevant business conditions.

A supplier offering the lowest price may not necessarily be the most economical choice. Production delays, transportation costs, and inventory shortages can all affect the final decision.

The agent needs to understand the whole situation rather than evaluate each factor separately.

An appropriately integrated agent could combine this information, evaluate different alternatives, and optimize its recommendations within a broader business context.

This is also where the relationship between digital intelligence and physical operations becomes visible.

A purchase order may exist as a digital record, but the goods themselves still need to be physically manufactured, transported, stored, and consumed.

SAP Build Process Automation

SAP Build Process Automation can support structured approval and execution processes integrated with SAP systems.

In our proposed architecture, the agent should understand the business situation, recommend a supplier, and pass its recommendation into the workflow for the next step.

The workflow should then review the recommendation and its business context, evaluating them against existing rules.

For example:

An approved supplier and a transaction below the delegated purchasing limit may qualify for automatic processing.

A transaction exceeding the spending limit requires additional authorization.

Missing or inconsistent information triggers a review.

A transaction outside approved business policies is blocked or escalated.

SAP Purchasing Approval and Decision Authority

In an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition environment, Flexible Workflow for Purchase Orders provides a concrete example of how enterprise approval boundaries can be established.

Depending on the configuration, a purchase order may be approved automatically or routed through one or more approval steps. This is how the workflow controls the different stages of approval.

For the proposed architecture, I would distinguish the agent's recommendation from the authorization mechanisms governing the actual purchase order.

SAP Build Process Automation could support additional orchestration, while SAP S/4HANA's Flexible Workflow for Purchase Orders and configured business authorizations would enforce the relevant purchasing approval controls.

This distinction matters because the agent's judgment should not become a substitute for the purchasing authority already established by the enterprise.

Proposed Procurement Process

The proposed process separates business judgment from authorization and execution.

Stage 1 - Business Context

SAP S/4HANA supplies relevant purchasing, inventory, supplier, and financial information through authorized interfaces.

Stage 2 - Agent Judgment

An agent developed with Joule Studio evaluates suppliers and recommends an option.

Stage 3 - Authority Verification

Configured enterprise controls and workflows check whether the transaction falls within delegated limits.

Stage 4 - Execution or Escalation

SAP Build Process Automation and authorized integrations proceed with an approved transaction or route it for further approval.

Stage 5 - Business Record

Relevant SAP business systems record the transaction and associated approvals.

In this example, the agent recommends Supplier C because its shorter delivery time could prevent a production delay.

However, that recommendation must pass the applicable authorization checks before it becomes an actual purchasing action.

These examples describe a proposed implementation pattern, not an out-of-the-box Decision Authority feature.

The architecture separates the agent's judgment from enforceable authorization controls and execution.

This separation matters because a model's conclusion should not automatically constitute permission to perform a restricted action.

3. Decision Boundaries

One question I frequently return to is whether an AI agent should be allowed to make autonomous decisions.

I do not believe there is a universal boundary applicable to every organization or every scenario.

The boundary depends on several layers: product capabilities, enterprise policies, compliance restrictions, user authorization, legal obligations, and other specific constraints.

Ultimately, the enterprise should determine which business decisions it is prepared to delegate, subject to the restrictions imposed by applicable law and the technology itself.

A technology provider can establish product-level security restrictions and operational safeguards. But it should not independently determine an organization's commercial risk appetite.

Consider two businesses using otherwise comparable purchasing agents.

Company A may permit autonomous purchasing only for routine replenishment.

Company B may authorize broader procurement decisions because management wants to move quickly in a competitive market.

The technical capability could be similar, while the delegated authority is very different.

This is not necessarily an inconsistency. It reflects different business objectives and governance choices.

Decision authority is therefore not merely a software configuration issue.

It is a boundary between organizational intentions, available technology, and the consequences of acting.

As trust, regulation, and operational experience develop, these boundaries may change.

The important architectural requirement is that they remain explicit, enforceable, and subject to appropriate human governance.

4. Procurement and Finance Agents

Multi-agent systems make these issues more visible.

Imagine a procurement agent recommending Supplier C because immediate delivery would protect the production schedule.

Meanwhile, a finance agent recommends Supplier B because of its lower purchase price.

Which agent should prevail?

I would not treat this as a universal technical hierarchy.

The answer depends on the enterprise's priorities, predefined authorization rules, and actual business constraints.

If the organization does not have sufficient available funds, approved credit, or budget, the purchasing agent cannot legitimately ignore those constraints.

Physical and financial limitations do not disappear simply because autonomous agents are involved.

But consider a different company.

Management may deliberately authorize aggressive purchases of scarce high-performance GPUs to secure future production capacity.

Meanwhile, this could also be a way to weaken competitors by securing limited market supply and disrupting their development plans.

Depending on market conditions, competitors might struggle to obtain the resources they need, potentially slowing their progress for months.

The company might accept higher costs and possible future price declines. It may not be short of money. Its priority could be maintaining its technological advantage, protecting its development pace, and widening the distance between itself and its competitors.

In this situation, a finance agent focused exclusively on minimizing current expenditure could produce a recommendation inconsistent with that objective.

The point is that both agents operate within a business system whose priorities must be established by the organization.

Internal agent coordination can therefore use policy-based priorities, financial constraints, and escalation rules to resolve conflicts.

I also believe there is room for agents representing different companies to negotiate. But internal coordination and external negotiation are two different relationships.

Internal Coordination and External Negotiation

External agent-to-agent interactions are different.

Imagine a steel manufacturer and a downstream industrial buyer, each represented by a purchasing or sales agent.

Both companies have their own business objectives, and they may need to buy or sell materials regularly.

The buyer's agent evaluates production demand, inventory, and maximum acceptable prices. Prices can fluctuate from day to day, so its purchasing decisions must respond to changing market conditions.

The supplier's agent evaluates production capacity, minimum acceptable prices, and delivery commitments.

These agents represent different companies and commercial entities. Their interests are not identical, but there is still common ground: one needs to sell materials, and the other needs to purchase them.

From a game-theoretic perspective, certain parts of their negotiation may resemble a zero-sum game. A lower price benefits the buyer but may reduce the supplier's margin.

However, the overall transaction is not necessarily zero-sum. Both sides may benefit from reaching an agreement.

The agents may negotiate quantities, prices, product specifications, and delivery schedules within independently authorized limits.

Meanwhile, each agent needs to understand its own company well enough to make better choices.

The buyer's agent should understand its company's production requirements, financial position, and future demand. The supplier's agent should understand its own costs, production capacity, inventory, and delivery commitments.

Neither agent necessarily controls the other.

Whether an agreement can be reached depends on whether their permitted trading conditions overlap.

This illustrates an important distinction in Agentic Commerce:

Internal coordination is shaped by organizational authority. External negotiation is shaped by the interaction of independently authorized business parties.

Agent-to-Agent communication can facilitate these interactions, but communication alone does not establish commercial authority.

I distinguish A2A communication as a technical mechanism from Agent-to-Agent Commerce as a form of commercial interaction. Agents exchanging information or coordinating tasks are not necessarily engaging in commerce. A2A Commerce involves agents representing different commercial parties, negotiating or conducting business activities within their respective authorization boundaries.

5. Business Judgment and Execution Efficiency

Enterprise AI discussions often emphasize automation efficiency.

This is understandable. Faster execution and lower operating costs offer measurable benefits.

However, I do not see efficiency alone as the ultimate source of long-term differentiation.

As computing resources and AI capabilities become more widely available, execution capacity may become increasingly accessible.

What could remain more difficult is the ability to understand how a business actually operates.

Consider a manufacturing company managing raw materials, finished goods, warehouses, transportation, and production schedules.

The company needs to arrange trucks, cargo, shipments, and manufacturing activities.

An agent may have access to inventory records and purchasing data. But genuinely useful judgment requires more than reading those records.

It needs to understand the business itself, the situation the company is facing, and the relationships between numbers, materials, and physical goods.

Transportation routes, market conditions, competitors' activities, production costs, and the company's future strategies may all affect what appears to be a straightforward operational decision.

A change in transportation schedules may affect production. A decision to increase inventory may influence available working capital. A competitor's actions may change purchasing priorities.

These relationships go far beyond data stored in the cloud.

Understanding the Physical World

Suppose the company has ten trucks.

Under normal conditions, four trucks transport incoming raw materials and six handle finished-product deliveries.

A sudden production increase may require reversing that allocation.

Should the company assign six trucks to incoming materials and four to outgoing shipments? Should it consolidate deliveries into fewer trips? Would a combination of road and air transportation be more economical for urgent orders?

These decisions depend on actual consumption rates, warehouse capacity, delivery commitments, transportation costs, and available resources.

The operational environment is constantly changing.

An enterprise AI agent capable of understanding these relationships may help coordinate resources more intelligently than a system that optimizes each individual workflow independently.

This is where I see significant potential for SAP-oriented enterprise AI.

Business systems contain important operational information, but an agent must turn that information into context-sensitive judgment.

It must also account for the physical world: goods require transportation, warehouses have limited space, production lines have capacity constraints, and money cannot be spent without authorization or financing.

An agent that understands these constraints may be better positioned to recommend practical decisions.

However, that depends on data quality, system integration, reliable reasoning, and controls. Greater access to enterprise data does not automatically produce better decisions.

6. Delegated Decision Authority

I expect enterprises to gradually delegate more decisions to AI agents.

Not because greater autonomy is inherently desirable, but because requiring human approval for every operational decision can create a bottleneck.

Initially, we wanted AI to improve efficiency, increase productivity, process more information, and simulate different business scenarios.

Human creativity and judgment remained important because people needed to connect this information, understand the broader situation, and make the final decision.

But humans need time to understand complex situations.

An individual cannot continuously process every piece of operational information. Missing a critical factor, or failing to understand how different business activities are connected, can lead to poor decisions and sometimes serious consequences.

If a human is placed at the end of an automated process simply to click Yes or No, it is difficult to assume that this person has fully understood everything the AI system evaluated.

Consider the difference in working hours.

AI agents can potentially operate twenty-four hours a day, continuously evaluating information and performing authorized tasks.

Human employees have limited working hours, perhaps eight hours a day under a conventional schedule.

If every routine decision needs to stop and wait for human approval, the organization may lose much of the efficiency it expected to gain.

The approval process itself becomes a bottleneck.

An organization that must pause for management approval at every routine purchasing, scheduling, or logistics adjustment may operate more slowly than one capable of delegating these decisions under well-defined policies.

This is more than a technical inconvenience. It can become a structural limitation on the organization's ability to improve its performance.

The same problem exists in traditional management. When every employee needs permission for every minor decision, the organization does not necessarily make better decisions. It may simply become slower.

The answer is not to eliminate management, but to define appropriate decision rights.

I believe the same principle applies to enterprise AI.

A capable agent should understand the organization's objectives, evaluate the available evidence, and make decisions within its delegated scope.

When an action exceeds that scope, additional authorization should be required.

Better judgment can support broader delegation, but broader delegation does not guarantee better judgment.

The long-term challenge is not simply to maximize autonomy. It is to build systems that understand the business well enough to make reliable decisions without requiring constant human intervention.

Conclusion

SAP technologies provide a useful foundation for exploring enterprise AI agents through actual business processes rather than abstract automation capabilities.

Joule Studio can support the development of intelligent agents. SAP S/4HANA provides enterprise business context. SAP Build Process Automation can support structured, controlled execution.

The additional architectural question is how decision authority should be established across these capabilities.

From my perspective, I want to emphasize Agent-to-Agent Commerce within the broader development of Agentic Commerce.

Agentic Commerce already includes a wide range of scenarios in which AI agents help individuals or businesses make purchasing decisions and complete transactions.

But Agent-to-Agent Commerce is more specific.

It involves agents representing different commercial parties, communicating, negotiating, and potentially carrying out transactions within their respective authorization boundaries.

This involves more than agents exchanging information or performing transactions.

It involves the gradual delegation of business judgment and decision-making within a broader system of legal, organizational, and operational responsibility.

I see this as a question about relationships and systems rather than an isolated technical challenge.

AI agents must understand the real world, not just numbers or digital records.

A purchasing decision involves real suppliers, warehouses, production capacity, transportation resources, financial commitments, and relationships between organizations.

The most competitive enterprise AI systems may not be those executing the greatest number of tasks or operating with the fewest restrictions.

They may be those that best understand the business, recognize real-world constraints, and exercise sound judgment within the authority they have been granted.

I believe the technical act of executing a decision may eventually become the simplest part of the process.

It could require little more than an API call or a button click.

But reaching the point where an enterprise can confidently authorize AI to make consequential decisions, trust its judgment, and allow it to improve without constantly reporting back to humans represents a much larger step.

That is not simply a technical transition.

It is a change in how organizations distribute authority, establish trust, and manage responsibility.

Enterprise AI is not only about automating what a company does. It is about understanding what the company should do, and under whose authority that decision can be made.

References

1. SAP Help Portal - Joule Studio
https://help.sap.com/docs/joule-studio/joule-studio/general-development-flow

2. SAP Help Portal - SAP Build Process Automation
https://help.sap.com/docs/build-process-automation/sap-build-process-automation/about

3. SAP Help Portal - SAP S/4HANA Cloud
https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_S4HANA_CLOUD

The procurement scenarios and Decision Authority architecture presented here are conceptual proposals, not descriptions of a deployed or validated SAP implementation.

About the Author

Shen Xu is an independent AI strategist and researcher focused on Decision Authority, Agentic Commerce, and Agentic Search Optimization. His research examines how AI agents reshape enterprise decision-making, commercial relationships, and digital markets.

entry.title: Working with Google Drive in SAP Build Process Automation: Find, Move and Rename Files
entry.content:
A hands-on walkthrough of the Google Drive activities in the Google Workspace SDK: searching for folders and files, moving a file into another folder, and renaming it.

Introduction

This is the sixth post in the series. The fourth post covered the one-time setup for Google Workspace: the OAuth client in Google Cloud Console, the External Authentication in Control Tower, and registering it on the Desktop Agent. The fifth used that setup to go through the Gmail activities. This post uses the same foundation for Google Drive.

Drive is a natural companion to Gmail. Attachments, invoices and reports often end up in Drive folders, and an automation needs to find them, organise them and sometimes rename them. We build one task automation that does exactly that, and along the way look at how the query field works, since it's what makes the search activities flexible.

Here's what we'll cover:

  • Listing folders and files, with and without a query
  • Finding a folder or file by name
  • Moving a file into a folder and renaming it, using IDs returned by the earlier steps
  • Writing Drive search queries

The Google Drive activity group is larger than what we use here. This post covers six of its activities, plus Select Google Authentication and Disconnect (Google).

The Drive Activities at a Glance

Searching for "drive" in the Tools panel lists the Google Drive activities: Rename File, Move File, Get Folder By Name, Get File By Name, Get File, Get Folder, Download File, Share To Email, Share To Domain, Share With Anyone, Delete File Or Folder and Upload File. The six highlighted in red are the ones used in this post, and they are all visible in the flow on the left.

 

The automation flow with the six Drive activities highlighted, next to the Google Drive activities in the Tools panel.

The flow is a straight line with no branches:

  • Step 1: Select Google Authentication.
  • Steps 2 to 5: Get Folder, twice (once without a query, once with one).
  • Steps 6 and 7: Get Folder By Name.
  • Steps 8 to 11: Get File, and Get File By Name.
  • Steps 12 to 15: Move File, then Rename File.
  • Step 16: Disconnect (Google).

Almost every activity is followed by a Log Message step that prints the activity's output, so we can see in the test console what Drive returned. All the Drive activities return their results in an output called metaDatas (or a simple true result for move and rename), and the number in front of it in the screenshots is the step that produced it.

Before You Start

  • Complete the setup from the fourth post. In Google Cloud Console, the Google Drive API must be enabled and the Drive scope added under Data Access.
  • In Control Tower, the External Authentication you select must include the Drive scope. The authentication in the fourth post only selected Gmail, so add Drive, then register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again so Google's consent screen asks for Drive access too.
  • The Drive scope gives access to all files in the Drive of the account you sign in with, so use a test account for experiments like this one.

For the test I created a Drive folder named SAP BPA TEST holding a few invoice PDFs, and, inside it, an empty folder named BPA Moved File that will receive the moved file. This is the Drive before the automation runs:

 

The SAP BPA TEST folder before the run: the empty BPA Moved File folder and three PDFs.

Part 1: Get Folder

Get Folder (Google Drive) searches for folders. It has three optional inputs: driveId (to target a specific drive), query, and timeout. The output, metaDatas, is the list of folders found.

  1. Get Folder without a query. I left all inputs empty. In my test, this returned every folder in my Drive.

 

Get Folder (Google Drive) with no query.

  1. Get Folder Log. A Log Message step takes metaDatas from step 2 as its message. I show this log step only once, because every other log step in the flow works the same way. The full list of folders it prints is long, so I'm not including that output.

 

Log Message printing the metaDatas output of step 2.

  1. Get Folder with a query. The second Get Folder step narrows the search with this query: mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' and name contains 'SAP'. It returns folders whose names contain a word starting with SAP.

 

Get Folder (Google Drive) - 2 with a query.

The log of this step (step 5) shows what came back: the SAP BPA TEST folder, with its ID, creation time and modification time. The IDs are hidden in the screenshot.

 

Log output of step 5: the matching folder.

Writing Drive Queries

The query field follows Google's Drive search query syntax, the same one the Drive API uses. A query has three parts: a term to search on, an operator, and a value, and parts can be combined with and, or, and not. Google's search query reference lists all valid terms and operators. These are the ones I find most useful:

  • name contains 'SAP' matches items whose name has a word beginning with SAP.
  • name = 'BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf' matches an exact name.
  • mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.folder' matches folders only. For PDFs, use mimeType = 'application/pdf'.
  • mimeType = 'application/pdf' and name contains 'Invoice' combines two conditions.
  • 'FOLDER_ID' in parents and trashed = false lists items directly inside a folder, excluding items in the Trash. Replace FOLDER_ID with the folder's ID.
  • modifiedTime > '2026-10-01T00:00:00' matches items modified after a date (RFC 3339 format).
  • fullText contains 'invoice' searches names, descriptions and the indexed content of files.

A few rules worth knowing:

  • Values go in single quotes. A single quote inside a value must be escaped with a backslash, for example name contains 'Bob\'s'.
  • name contains only matches the beginning of words. Google's example: for an item named HelloWorld, name contains 'Hello' finds it, but name contains 'World' does not.
  • To leave out items in the Trash, add trashed = false.

In this post I tested the name and mimeType terms. The other terms are documented by Google for the Drive API, but I'd recommend trying them in a test folder first.

Part 2: Get Folder By Name

When you only know a folder's name, Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) is simpler than writing a query. Its required input is name, which I set to BPA Moved File. The name doesn't have to be complete; in my tests a partial name matched as well.

 

Get Folder By Name (Google Drive) with the folder name.

The log of step 7 shows one folder returned: BPA Moved File. Its ID is what the Move File step uses later.

 

Log output of step 7: the BPA Moved File folder.

Part 3: Get File and Get File By Name

Files have their own pair of activities. Get File (Google Drive) has the same inputs as Get Folder (driveId, query, timeout) and returns files. With no query it returns files from the whole Drive, so I don't show its log, which is a long list.

 

Get File (Google Drive) with no query.

Get File By Name (Google Drive) takes a required fileName. I used BPA_Demo, a partial name, so it matches every file whose name starts that way.

 

Get File By Name (Google Drive) with a partial file name.

Because the name was partial, the log of step 11 lists several files: BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, BPA_Demo_Invoice_Approval_01.pdf and BPA_Demo_Invoice_AutoApproval_02.pdf. In this run, the first item in the list was BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf, which is the file I want to move.

 

Log output of step 11: the files matching the partial name.

Part 4: Move File

Move File (Google Drive) needs two IDs, both taken from earlier steps:

  • fileId: metaDatas[0].id from step 10, the first file returned by Get File By Name.
  • destinationFolderId: metaDatas[0].id from step 6, the folder returned by Get Folder By Name.

The two steps that provide the IDs are marked in red in the flow. The output result is true when the move succeeded.

 

Move File (Google Drive), with its two IDs coming from steps 10 and 6.

Part 5: Rename File

Rename File (Google Drive) takes fileId and newName. A move doesn't change a file's ID, so I reuse metaDatas[0].id from step 10 and rename the file to Moved_File.pdf. Include the extension in the new name, because the name you enter is the whole name.

 

Rename File (Google Drive), reusing the file ID from step 10.

The logs for steps 13 and 15 simply print the true result of Move File and Rename File:

 

Move File Log and Rename File Log, both printing true.

Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google)

The last step, Disconnect (Google), closes the connection to Google when the work is done.

Running It

I ran the automation from the designer. The test console prints the results of each log step. Some entries are hidden, because they contain names and IDs from my Drive. The final two entries are the true results of Move File and Rename File. The warning at the end only says the testing session has stopped.

 

The test console, with IDs and some names hidden.

In Drive, BPA_Demo_Invoice.pdf is no longer in the SAP BPA TEST folder:

 

The SAP BPA TEST folder after the run.

Inside the BPA Moved File folder, the file is now called Moved_File.pdf:

 

The BPA Moved File folder after the run, holding the renamed file.

Things to Keep in Mind

  • Check which item you take from the list. Partial names can match several items, and the steps above use metaDatas[0], the first one. Here the first match was the file I wanted, but I wouldn't rely on the order. Use a more specific name or query, or look through metaDatas for the item you need.
  • Guard against empty results. If a search finds nothing, a later step that reads metaDatas[0] has nothing to read. Add a condition after each search, as in the Gmail posts.
  • Add error handling. These activities can throw a GoogleDriveError. I left out Try / Catch to keep the flow readable, but you should wrap the Drive steps in one in a real automation.
  • Avoid logging full lists. Get Folder and Get File without a query return everything they can find, which makes long logs in a large Drive. Use a query to narrow results.
  • Treat logs as sensitive. They include file and folder IDs, and for files, download links. Hide them in screenshots you share.
  • Test-mode token expiry. As mentioned in the fourth post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again.

Wrapping Up

With a handful of activities, a BPA automation can search a Drive by name or by query, organise files into folders and rename them, all driven by the IDs that earlier steps return. The same Google setup from the fourth post serves both Gmail and Drive. The other Drive activities in the Tools panel (Download, Share, Delete and Upload) aren't covered in this post.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.
